speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Well, I found out very quickly from the Minister of Militia and Defence. It seems to me that my right hon. friend is hypercritical when he suggests that a minister of the Crown must know all these details about the proceedings of a commission that is carrying on its work. The commission is sitting for the purpose of holding a public investigation. I understand that the representatives of the press were present this morning; they knew about it, there iff nothing secret about it and if it is desired, Sir Charles Davidson will no doubt send to my right hon. friend, or to any of his followers whom he may designate, notice of the time and the place at which the commission will sit for the purpose of this, or any other investigation. I am glad that my hon. friend the member for North Cape Breton (Mr. COMMONS
McKenzie) has arrived at the conclusion that the Royal Commission composed of Sir William Meredith and Mr. Justice Duff is an efficient commission. Great objection was taken to the appointment of that commission for the purpose of investigating the matters they now have in hand, but my hon. friend from North Cape Breton is evidently satisfied with the commission so far, for he suggests that a further inquiry be referred to them.
As to the inquiry now before the Royal Commission, I might point out that it relates to an expenditure by the Government of the United Kingdom, whereas the inquiry with which Sir Charles Davidson is charged relates to matters with which the Government of Canada is concerned. For that reason, therefore, it was more proper to refer this matter to Sir Charles Davidson than to a commission which was appointed for the purpose of investigating expenditures made, not by this Government, but by the Government of the United Kingdom. There was this further reason for referring this matter to Sir Charles Davidson. Certain persons who are not usually in Ottawa, and who might be able to give necessary evidence in this inquiry, are in Ottawa at the present .time. It could hardly be expected that Sir William Meredith and Mr. Justice Duff would interrupt the proceedings they are now carrying on, for the purpose of taking up this inquiry. On the other hand, Sir Charles Davidson was in a position to take it up at once, and secure the evidence of witnesses who are now available in the city of Ottawa. It was therefore more convenient, and more in the public interest, as we thought, to refer this matter to Sir Charles Davidson rather than to Sir William Meredith and Mr. Justice Duff. The Government have absolute confidence both in the one commission and in the other; we have absolutely no choice between them. The only thing the Government would desire from either commission would be an impartial and thorough inquiry, and it would secure that inquiry whether the matter was referred to Sir William Meredith and Mr. Justice Duff or to Sir Charles Davidson.
Coming to the points which my hon. friend has made, he has alluded to the Auditor General's letter, and to the fact that no Order in Council seems to have been passed. This subject first came to my attention in the first or second week of February last, when some further information which had been asked for was received

from the Department of Militia and Defence. In consequence of the report then received still further information was asked for, and this did not come to hand until the first week of March, and did not come to my attention and was not read by me until after the Minister of Militia and Defence had left for England. I therefore did not read the information which has been brought down and laid on the table of the House, and which is contained in a memorandum from the Quartermaster General, until after the Minister of Militia and Defence had left for England. The question was discussed in the public press, and it was alluded to by my right hon. friend who leads the Opposition on the occasion when the Minister of Militia and Defence made a statement to the House with regard to the allegations of the hon. member for Richmond. It seemed to me then that as discussion had taken place and criticism had been made in the public press, and as my right hon. friend who leads the Opposition had made certain statements-I will not say insinuations-with regard to the matter, the subject was deserving of inquiry. We were aware then that witnesses whose testimony might be important and even necessary, would probably be very soon available in Ottawa, and for that reason	no further	proceedingswere	taken	upon the	report to
Council, arid the matter stood until, the inquiry, as to which I spoke to the Minister of Justice about ten days ago, could be made. That inquiry is now proceeding. Therefore, so far as this matter calls for an inquiry, I have only to say that an inquiry is already in progress before a gentleman of the highest integrity, ability and experience, and in whose capacity to make an impartial and thorough inquiry I am sure the country will have absolute confidence, and in whom the Government has the like confidence.
My hon. friend not only makes a demand for an inquiry, but proceeds to censure the Minister of Militia and Defence, and incidentally the Government, for the course which has been adopted. Let us look for a moment at the circumstances to which the hon. gentleman has called attention. In the first place he says that no one seemed to know to whom the ammunition was sold, or where it was going. The hon. gentleman is not well advised in making that statement, because the documents upon their face show that the ammunition was

sold to Vickers; Limited, and the shipping documents which have,been brought down and laid upon the Table show that the ammunition was shipped in care of Vickers, Limited, London, England; therefore, so far as the person to whom it was sold and the place to which it was shipped are concerned, there is no, warrant for the statement which my hon. friend has made.
He then goes on to suggest that the price at which this ammunition was sold was altogether too low. He suggests, rather than states, that it was perfectly good ammunition suitable for use by the troops at the front, and that ammunition of that type is now costing $34 or thereabouts per 1,000 rounds. He says in effect that the Minister of Militia and Defence sold for $20 per 1,000 rounds ammunition which had to be purchased at the price of $34 per 1,000 rounds. Either my hon. friend has not examined the papers or he was not desirous of making a fair and reasonable statement to the House. I shall take occasion to quote from the documents to show precisely what the facts are. As a matter of fact, only four months before this war broke out this same ammunition was offered for $12 per 1,000 rounds to the Ross Rifle Company, for testing purposes, and was refused by them. Further, the price for the same ammunition fixed by the responsible officers of the Department of Militia and Defence before this war broke out was $10 per 1,000 roundB, which is one-half of the first cost, as I am informed. This is the very same ammunition for which this country is to-day receiving $20 per 1,000 rounds.
It is worth while perhaps for me to refer to the report of the Quartermaster-General with Tegard to this matter. The regulations for the Army Ordnance Service, part 2, paragraphs 552-3, define the steps to be taken in regard to ammunition which has been declared unserviceable, and reads as follows :
Small arm ammunition, having been sentenced " Unserviceable " by the Inspecting Ordnance Officer or other proper authority, and the sentence having been approved, will be dealt with as follows: the bullets will be extracted, the cartridges will then be fired off and loose cordite will be burned. Where it is for any reason impossible to destroy ammunition in the above manner, it will be drowned in deep water.
A few years ago the Minister of Militia caused a very careful investigation to be made with regard to the ammunition in stock in this country. The report of the British experts who made that investigation has been brought down and laid upon the table of the House. It is proper that I should read a portion of that report:
As to small arms ammunition, we do not recommend the continuance of ringing on new ammunition. We regard the ringing as a satisfactory method of Checking the blow-backs to which Dominion Arsenal '303 cartridges have in the past been peculiarly liable. Cases recently manufactured-with cap chamber better formed and freer from scores, etc.-do not require ringing, and we do not consider that in [DOT]303 cases of future manufacture, any necessity should arise for this treatment, which should be regarded only as a means of overcoming defective manufacture.
The report is a very long one and indicates that ammunition manufactured during certain years, more particularly when my hon. friends opposite were responsible for the management of the Dominion Arsenal, was not of a quality which would justify its use in active service. The report continues:
Some 40,000 to 50,000 cartridges have been rejected on examination after ringing.
I do not precisely understand the operation of ringing, and it will be explained by my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Sam Hughes). It was a device for making defective ammunition serviceable by overcoming certain defects which had occurred in its manufacture. The report continues:
We would suggest that these be visually examined for elim.nation of scored cases, etc., and used for machine gun practice only.
Further on the report proceeds:
Ammunition subsequent to February, 1908, to be ringed, visually examined for ringing and for external scores, and for elimination of the old e.g. (07) cases, and subject to firing proof before reissue. For each lot of 200,000 rounds, 1,000 rounds should ibe taken for proof; if a burst occurs, a second proof of 1,000 should be taken of the lot in question and also of the lot immediately preceding and the one immediately following. We do not think that ammunition manufactured in and prior to February, If08, is likely to be rendered serviceable even after ringing on recount of the uncertain annealing and its liability to bursts, and we are of opinion that the ammunition should be broken up and the cases might be used for blank and a certain saving thereby effected.
I want my hon. friend and the House generally to understand that of the 3,000,000 rounds which have been sold 2,000,000 are of the character which I have described. Those 2,000,000 rounds were ordered by the Barlow reportr-the report of British officers brought to this country for the purpose of making a thorough examination of our ammunition-not to be ringed, not

to be used for any purpose, but to be broken, up, and it was recommended that the cases should be used for blanks and a certain saving thereby effected. Therefore, so far as these 2,000,000 rounds were concerned, they were absolutely condemned by the Barlow report, and the 4 p.m. Minister of Militia and Defence, when the matter came before him, wrote the word " destroy," because it was obvious that that ammunition was not fit to be used in active service, nor even for practice.
Now, a precis of what took place will be found in the report of the quartermaster general, which 'has been brought down to the House, and which, after setting forth the regulations of the Army Ordnance Service, goes on to say:
The Barlow report condemned as unserviceable all '303 ammunition manufactured prior to February, 1908, and recommended same to be destroyed.
I have just read a quotation from that report. Then the following memoranda are noted:
Memo, from Director of Artillery proposing selling all Mark VI ammunition of five years of age and older at half price, dated 24th October, 1911.
Submission along this line to Militia Council by Master General of Ordnance, approved by Militia Council, dated 15th November, 1911.
Notification by Director of Artillery to Principal Ordnance Officer of decision of Council to sell and asking for insertion in Militia Order, dated 18th November, 1911.
A militia order to that effect was made thereupon in the same month.
Telegram, 4th of May, 1914, from manager, Ross Rifle Company asking what quantity of ammunition department would sell.
That was followed by a recommendation of the Master General of Ordnance to sell it, and there was thereupon a reply from the deputy minister to the Ross Rifle Co., offering to sell 10,000,000 rounds at $12 per thousand rounds. That offer was dated the 18th of May, 1914.
The next document to which the Quartermaster General calls attention is a memorandum dated the 29th July, 1914, from the Quartermaster General to the Master General of Ordnance, suggesting that this ammunition be destroyed by drowning. The destruction of ammunition by drowning simply mean that it is thrown into deep water where no harm can result from it. The suggestion was that this ammunition should be disposed of in that way rather than by the method proposed in the Barlow report. It will be remembered that the

commission made a recommendation as to taking out and utilizing the cordite, and thereby effecting some saving. My hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence says that the proposal to break up the ammunition and save the cordite was in virtue of a departmental regulation and not a suggestion of the Barlow Commission.
The next document, which is dated July 30, 1914, just before the war broke out, is a reply from the Ross Rifle Company refusing the offer of sale at price quoted.
There are some of these documents which I think it might be of interest for me to read to the House. I am afraid they are not arranged here in chronological order, but I will read them just as they are, and hon. gentlemen, I think, will sufficiently understand the situation.
The first document that I have here is dated January 8, 1914, and is a report from General Morrison, who is now at the front:
According to tbe findings of the Barlow report on the Dominion Arsenal and its output all "303 ammunition made prior to February, 1908, is condemned as unserviceable, and it is recommended that this ammunition should be destroyed.
During the past summer some of this ammunition was used by the Royal Canadian Regiment at Halifax with very bad results, though no serious accidents happened.
I would suggest that orders be issued that no more of the ammunition made prior to February, 1908, should be issued to or used by troops, pending the decision of the minister as to what disposition is to be made of it.
Regarding all Mark VI ammunition made subsequent to January 31st, 1908, the report recommends that it should all be tested before being passed as serviceable. No action has yet been taken by the Honourable the minister, in council regarding this recommendation, possibly because until the arrival of Captain Gordon Ogilvie from Woolwich to take over the appointment of inspector of small arm ammunition there was no officer available to carry out the tests. Further action on this will be reported on at an early date.
Hon. gentlemen should bear in mind that all this ammunition which has been sold is what is known as Mark VI, which is only intended for Mark II Ross rifle. The authorized Ro-ss rifle at the present time is the Mark III Ross rifle.' Therefore, not one single round of this ammunition, even if it had not been condemned, could have been used in active service at the front because our troops are armed, not with the Mark II Ross rifle,-but with the Mark III Ross rifle. I consulted with the Master General of Ordnance himself, and he told me that not one single round of any ammunition of Mark VI should be issued for service at the front, as if would be unsuitable; and the ammunition which must be

issued for troops at the front is Mark VII ammunition. The only ammunition sold was Mark VI, and it included two million rounds which had been condemned as absolutely unserviceable. The next document I wish to read is dated 24th October, 1911. It is signed by Major General Elliott, a British Officer of long experience, who entered the Canadian service some years ago and whose work has been thoroughly satisfactory, indicating that his capacity and experience are all that could be desired:
With reference to your return of .303-inch ball ammunition; it is suggested as ammunition over 5 years old is liable to deteriorate that all S.A.A. of dates up to and including 1906 beginning with the oldest should be sold at half price. This will make more certain of a turnover which is absolutely necessary, and will it is thought be appreciated by all ranks interested in rifle shooting and also by Rifle Associations and Cadet Corps.
It is at any rate better to make use of old though serviceable ammunition rather than to keep it so long that it becomes useless and has to be destroyed. An instance of this as you know has lately occurred.
Hon. members will bear in mind that this was nearly four years ago, and his suggestion was that they should begin to dispose of the ammunition of 1905 manufacture which, at the present time, would correspond, roughly speaking, with that manufactured in 1909. A memorandum upon that was made by Major-General Hallick, prinicpal Ordnance Officer, in the following words:
It is necessary before giving instruc. tions, to ascertain from S.O.O.'s the date of manufacture of all ammunition on charge which in the consolidated return is shown as " prior to 1903 This is in hand.
It is assumed you will obtain council's authority for the proposed reduction in price for sales?
Then I come to a report of the Master General of the Ordnance which was confirmed by the Militia Council. The date of the submission of this report was 10th November, 1911. The report is in the following words:
The Master-General of the Ordnance makes the following submission for approval of the Minister in Militia Council.
Small Arm ammunition over five years old should be sold at half price.
This will obviate the possibility of this ammunition having to be destroyed owing to age and consequent deterioration, will ensure a proper turn over which is not 1 h . case at present, and will probably be app eciated by Rifle Associations and Cadet Corps.
That was presented to the Militia Council, and on 15th November, 1911, it was approved by the Militia Council, as will appear from this minute:
The Master-General of the Ordnance:
Your submission in this case was considered at the meeting of the Militia Council held this day, and approved.
E. F. Jarvis, Secretary,
The Militia Council.
Other departmental minutes and memoranda with regard to the subject were made, and finally the following report was made by the Quartermaster-General and was embodied, as I understand it, in Militia Orders:
Price of '303" ball cartridges of old manufacture.
In future, issues on payment by the Canadian Ordnance Corps of *303" ball cartridges of over 5 years manufacture will be made at half price, viz., $10 (ten dollars) per thousand rounds.

The Ross Rifle Company, as appears by the correspondence, refused to purchase at the price of $12 and the proposed eale wa6 not carried out. I may observe also that the ammunition which it wa6 proposed to sell to the Ross Rifle Company was 1908 and 1909 ammunition, whereas the two million rounds ,to which I have alluded was three years older, having been manufactured in 1905 and 1906.
The result, therefore, is that the Department has sold at $20 per thousand rounds ammunition declared absolutely unservic-able by the Barlow report and ordered to be destroyed; ammunition which was three years older than the ammunition which was offered to the Ross Rifle Company in May 1914 at $12 per thousand rounds. I think that if these facts are borne in mind by the hon. gentlemen, they will dispose of any question as to adequacy of price.
The report which I was about to read is a report from Col. J. F. Macdonald for the Quartermaster-General.	It is dated
July 29, 1914, and is as follows:
Destruction of ammunition of date of manufacture prior to February 1908. With reference to folios 110 to 114, the S.O.O.-
S.O.O. means the Senior Ordnance Officer.
With reference to folios 110 to 114, the S.O.O. -5th division, was instructed to hand over to the superintendent of the Dominion Arsenal the stock of ammunition referred to on folio 41. He now reports that the superintendent has neither time, facilities nor accommodation for taking over this ammunition, but that he, the superintendent, stated that it may be possible to take it over about the 1st of October for salvage, provided, in the meantime, he sees that it will lead to economy.
It therefore seems doubtful whether the Dominion Arsenal will be able to take over

the ammunition, and as the storage accommodation taken up by it is very urgently required for serviceable ammunition, and the boxes in which it Is packed are required for packing ammunition now being manufactured, would it not be preferable to have all this condemned ammunition destroyed by drowning or otherwise?
Please see my minute, folio 114, in this connection, to which you do not seem to have replied.
J. F. Macdonald,
Lit-Colonel, for Major General, Quartermaster-General.
There is a minute made upon that report by Gen. Hughes, personally, on the 6th day of October, 1914-I am not sure whether that is the correct date or not- which is just one word: "Destroy" of which the director of artillery made a note.
I might read, although it does not come in order of date, the letter of the Ross Rifle Company refusing the offer to sell at $12.00. It is under date of July 30, 1914, and is as follows:
Col. Eugene Fiset,
Deputy Minister,
Department of Militia and Defence, Ottawa, Ont.
Sir,-Your letter of July 6th H.Q. " C " 1402 was duly received but acknowledgment was delayed owing to the writer's absence.
In view of the fact that we received a quotation from Ottawa, under date of February 26, of $10 per 1,000 for 500,000 rounds of .303 ammunition, it will be impossible for us to avail ourselves of your quotation of May 18th, viz. $12.75 per 1,000, which is $2.75 per 1,000 in excess of the former offer.
We beg to remain, Sir,

Ross Rifle Company.

Secretary.
It is perfectly true, as the hon. member for North Victoria and Cape Breton has said, that there was a note, concurred in, I think, by the chief of the General Staff and the Deputy Minister of Militia and Defence, that none of this defective ammunition should be sold. I have that under my hand, and I should like to refer to its exact terms. It was on the 13th of October, 1914; I might as well read it:
Under the existing circumstances, low stock of ammunitidn, do you not think it would be wiser to hold this ammunition until such time as the stock in depots is brought up to normal condition?
See folio 122 hereof.
D. A. Macdonald,
Major-General,
Quartermaster-General.
The following note appears under that: " We should not dispose of one single round. (Signed) E. F„ D. M. 15th October, 1914."	" E. F." means the Deputy

Minister of Militia and Defence. A further memorandum by Colonel Gwatkin, now General Gwatkin, was as follows:
With reference to folio 122, the situation has changed since the word "Destroy" was written; and the order, unless repeated, should not be carried out.
Then further on:	"Noted. Necessary
action taken." . All these memoranda are based on the report of the Quartermaster General, which declared that would be wiser to hold this ammunition until such time as the stock in depots had been brought up to normal condition. Let us see what the condition was at the time the war broke out-because a statement with regard to that is brought down and included in the return. My hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence desires to know whether this should be made public. 1 say no. I made this public in the face of the advice of the Chief of the General Staff, the Deputy Minister of Militia and Defence and the Master General of Ordnance. I felt that I was compelled to do so by reason of the insinuations and virtual charges made in this House, moTe particularly by my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. Notwithstanding the advice of these officials, I was determined that this information should be brought down and the facts made known, although the publication of those facts may be a detriment ito the public interest. If hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House are determined to spend their time in seeking to pry into matters of this character with regard to which they are not fully informed, and to make charges and insinuations with regard .to them, it is necessary, in order that public opinion in this country should be quieted, that we should make matters public that otherwise would not be made public. Therefore I felt it my duty to bring this information down and to place the actual conditions before the people.
On the first day of August there was in stock of Mark VI ammunition 36,418,160 rounds and of Mark VII ammunition 3,534,571 rounds, a total of 39,952,731 rounds. Hon. gentlemen will observe that we had on the first day of August, 1914, a very large supply of ammunition suitable for the -Mark II Ross rifle, and a very small amount of ammunition sujitable for the Mark III Ross rifle, which is the rifle used on active service, as it has superseded Mark II. We sent forward, to be used, as we understood, for practice purposes, a
very considerable amount of Mark VI ammunition when the first Canadian contingent went forward. So that on the 31st December, 1914, the supply stood in this way:
Rounds.
Mark VI	 14,936,304
Mark VII	 4,161,556
A total of	 19,097,860
As compared with 39,952,731 rounds on the 1st day of August. In other words, we had decreased by about twenty-one and a half million rounds the supply of Mark VI, and we had increased by about 600,000 rounds the supply of Mark VII. The decrease was due to shipment of large quantities to Great Britain. On the 31st day of March, 1916, the supply stands as follows:

We have decreased by about five million rounds the Mark VI ammunition, which is not suitable for use in active service at the front with the Mark III Ross rifle, the standard rifle of the Canadian forces; and we have increased by nearly eight and a half million rounds the supply of the Mark VII ammunition, which is the ammunition designed for use with the rifle with which our troops are armed for active service. So then I venture to think that, taking things i as they were in the autumn of 1914 and as they are to-day, the condition alluded to by the quartermaster general has been brought about, as the supply of ammunition has been brought up to very much more than normal for the Mark III Ross rifle.
Under the circumstances, the course which was taken by the Minister of Militia and Defence was this: We have still in stock in Canada 10,000,000 rounds of Mark VI ammunition. I have conferred with authority as high as any recognized in this country respecting the supply of that type of ammunition which should be kept on ' hand; and the amount named to me was 5,000,000 rounds. This, as I have said, is suited for the old type of Ross rifle, and is not so suitable for the new type. Instead of 5,000,000 rounds of this kind of ammunition, we have to-day nearly 10,000,000 rounds; and in addition to that we have twelve and a half million rounds of Mark VII ammunition, which is suitable for use with the improved

Ross rifle for active service. Under the circumstances, hon. gentlemen on the other side, on the strength of newspaper rumours, have seen fit to make charges or insinuations in this matter, and we have thought it desirable that all the documents should be brought down, even though, in the ordinary course, they would not be brought down as they give certain information with which we would prefer that the enemy should not be made acquainted.
And we have done more than that; we have passed an Order in Council directing that there shall be a full inquiry into all the circumstances of this case, and that inquiry is now proceeding. Under the circumstances, considering that an inquiry has already been directed and is now proceeding, my hon. friend's motion is inopportune for two reasons:	In the first place,
the inquiry which he asks for is now being carried on and, in the second place, it is a most unusual course thaj; any gentleman in this House while a matter is under inquiry by a responsible tribunal, should see fit, without waiting for the report of that commission, to propose a motion condemning the Government and especially condemning one of its members. It would have been in better taste, and the time of the House would not have been wasted, if my hon. friend had awaited the conclusion of that inquiry and reserved the motion he now proposes until we had before us the information which will be afforded by that inquiry when made. I need hardly add that, under the circumstances, we cannot accept the motion of my hon. friend, because an effective inquiry is now being proceeded with. When that inquiry has been made and the report upon it is in the possession of hon. gentlemen of this House, it will be quite time enough for any hon. gentleman on the other side of the House to come forward with a vote of censure.

Mr. Speaker, my right hon. friend (Sir Robert Borden) opened his remarks by complaining that he had not received the usual courtesy which is extended from one side to the other whenever a subject is to be taken up which is not already on the Orders of the Day. The little discussion which took place between him and the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) showed that there was no cause for complaint on his part. It has been shown that my right hon. friend did receive ample

notification, because last Monday-this is Saturday-and last Monday the member for Cape Breton informed my right hon. friend by letter that on that very day, last Monday, he would ask for an inquiry into this matter, specifying that he would ask that this matter be referred to the commission composed of Sir William Meredith and Mr. Justice Duff. Surely, after the many occasions on which, during the present session, this matter has already been brought to the attention of the House, my right hon. friend should have known what was meant; and so it seems to me that his complaint was not well founded.
I call my right hon. friend's attention to this, that time and again during the present session he has stated that if any member had charges to make against anybody, against the Government or any of its members, the moment an hon. member would take the responsibility of making the charges, most ample investigation would be offered and given. If, Sir, there is a case which requires investigation, and the most ample investigation at that, it is the very matter which we now have in hand. Records which have already been brought down show that, some time during last year, the Minister of Militia took upon himself to dispose of a certain quantity of small ammunition. He had no warrant, he had no authority for doing so, the thing was absolutely illegal. What he sold was not the property of Gen. Sir Sam Hughes; it was the property of the 'Government, and the Government alone could dispose of it. What was his authority, what reason was given? My right hon. friend has given no reason at all for the conduct of his colleague in the matter. Whether the minister acted upon his own motion, without even consulting his colleagues verbally, does not appear. The first thing we know of this is that a communication was sent by the Auditor General to the Minister of Finance on the 3rd of April, 1916, calling the attention of the Minister of Finance to the fact, some time prior to the 31st of December last, this department sold through Colonel J. Wesley Allison, without the authority of the Governor in Council, over 3,000,000 rounds of ammunition at $20 per thousand rounds, and he concluded in this way:
I have therefore to request that you will obtain the approval of the Governor in Council for the sale, and that you will also let me know why the rate was fixed at $20 per thousand rounds.
It is very strange that amongst the papers brought down, the authority of the Governor General in Council for the sale of

that ammunition is not given. The only thing I find in the record is a recommendation of the Minister of Militia, dated 5th of January, 1916, to His Royal Highness the Governor General in Council, which is in the following words:
January 5, 1916.
To His Royal Highness the
Governor General in Council,
The undersigned has the honour to submit for the consideration and approval of Your Royal Highness in Council an application from Vickers Limited for the purchase of 4,985,900 rounds of S. A. ammunition, mark VI. This is part of the stock of mark VI ammunition, which, under suspicion, was not allowed to be used with rifles in Canada. The price of the ammunition to be $20 per thousand rounds. This ammunition, while rejected for rifle use.
Mark the -words-
-for rifle use is, however, reported to be suitable for testing of Vickers machine guns which are manufactured in very large numbers in England.
The matter is respectfully submitted.
Sam Hughes,
Major General,
Minister of Militia and Defence.
That is the recommendation to council dated 5th January last. The report in answer to the motion passed by the House was brought in about three weeks ago. No Order in Council is found in the papers and as far as we know to this day there is no Order in Council. A few days ago my hon. friend from Pietou (Mr. Macdonald) asked why this Order in Council had not been, brought down. If I remember the answer of the right hon. the Prime Minister correctly, it was then stated that the Order in Council had not been passed because the matter had been brought to the attention of the Council in the absence of the Minister of Militia. Mystery piles upon mystery in this matter. The recommendation was made and sent to Council apparently on the 5th January. January passed away, February passed away, March passed away. For three months the Minister of Militia was here attending to his duties; he sailed for England in the last days of March or the first days of April, I do not know which; he was away for some three weeks, he has been back now for three weeks and to this day the Government has not legalized such an illegal matter as the sale of the property of the Government by the Minister of Militia. What age are we *living in? Is this Parliamentary Government, or is it not Parliamentary Government? Do I understand that the members of the Government will allow one of their colleagues to dispose of the property of the
country illegally and without a tittle of authority? That is the position in which we are at the present time.
My right hon. friend says that there are certain matters which ought not to be brought to the attention of the country because they affect the war. He gave us the information as to the amount of ammunition which was held by the country at one time, and the amount which is held to-day, and he says he did this in defiance of the advice of his officers to allay the suspicions of the Opposition. When and where have we asked for any information as to the amount of the stock of ammunition which is held by the Government? We have never inquired into that, we do not want to know. That is the business of the Government and in regard to that it ought to be trusted. But, we do want to know under what circumstances a part of the stock which should have been held for the country was disposed of to that philanthropist, Mr. J. W. Allison. The answer given by the Prime Minister to-day is not only insufficient but-and I do not want to characterize it too strongly-it is in absolute defiance of the law of Parliament. We should know where we stand to-day. Do the Government approve of their colleagues disposing of the property of the Government as he has done or do they not? What is the reason that to-day we have not the sanction of the Government for this matter? We should know whether or not the Government approve of the action of their colleague and if they do approve of it then they should legalize it because the thing is illegal. If they do not approve of it they should tell us why they do not approve of it and they should act accordingly. The whole defence which is set up by the Prime Minister to-day with regard to this sale is simply this, that there was a certain stock of ammunition which was deficient and which had been condemned by the authorities. But, I do not understand that the ammunition which was condemned by the authorities -is the ammunition which was disposed of under this recommendation of the Minister of Militia to Council, is the ammunition which he has sold to that philanthropist and patriot, Mr. J. W. Allison, because he does not say in that recommendation to his colleagues that he wants to dispose of all the ammunition which was found defective. No, he says it is " suspicious." He speaks of .such part of the stock of Mark VI ammunition as was under sus-

picion and he says that it was not allowed to be used with rifles in Canada; that it is suspicious and should not be used in the field. Yet, it has some virtue in it because he goes on to say that:
The price of the ammunition to be $20 per thousand rounds. This ammunition, while rejected for rifle use-
Mark the words-
-is however reported to be useful for the testing of Vickers machine guns now being manufactured in very large numbers in England.
If this ammunition was useful to Vickers for the testing of their machine guns, why was it sold to Vickers and not to the Imperial authorities? The Imperial authorities wanted this ammunition just as much as Vickers-Maxim wanted it and the charge which we make against the Government in this matter is that this stock was disposed of to a private individual, and that this Government had no right to authorize the disposal of this ammunition to anybody but the Imperial authorities. If they had power to do so, an Order in Council stating that the Government had that power ought to have been passed. There is on record in this return which has been brought down, the rule laid down by the Quartermaster General, General Macdonald, approved by the Deputy Minister oi Militia and Defence, that no ammunition should be disposed of to anybody. In the face of this it was disposed of. Leaving aside altogether the fact that it was disposed of to such a person as Mr. John Wesley Allison, do hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, in times of war, believe that we should dispose of the stock of ammunition that we have, deficient or not deficient, useful or not useful, to anybody but the Imperial authorities if we do not require to use it ourselves? I submit that in this time of war, it is nothing short of a crime against the country that we should deplete our stock of ammunition by selling it to anybody. But who is that body? It is Mr. J. W. Allison who represents himself to be acting as a philanthropist while acting for the Vickers-Maxim Company.
It is said that the ammunition was sold to the Vickers-Maxim Company for testing purposes. I call the minister's attention to the letter of the Auditor General in which he says that he had reason to believe that the ammunition was disposed of finally through somebody to the Imperial authorities; that is to say that the ammunition, instead of being sold directly by the Gov-
[Sir Wilfrid I.aurier. j
ernment here to the Imperial authorities, was sold to private individuals, or through the agency of Mr. J. Wesley Allison. The Auditor General in his letter, makes use of this language:
The department has been buying ammunition since the declaration of war at $33 per thousand rounds and has also been manufacturing ammunition at the Dominion Arsenal at a cost of $34.60 per thousand rounds; consequently, there has been a loss to the Government in this transaction of over $45,000.
It is alleged that this ammunition has been sold to Vickers, Limited, for testing purposes. I can hardly credit that statement, owing to the magnitude of the sale; but if it were sold, why was it sold at such a low rate, and why was it necessary to obtain the services of Colonel Allison? Mark this: the Auditor General can hardly believe that this ammunition was sold to Vickers, Limited, for testing purposes. Well, for my part, I am rather disposed to agree, until better informed, with the suspicion of the Auditor General. Vickers, Ltd., were intending to buy 5,000,000 rounds of ammunition at $20 per 1,000 rounds. Some 3,000,000 rounds had been delivered, for which they would have to pay $60,000, and there is evidence on record that some $20,000 was paid. Now, $60,000 seems to be a very large sum to pay for ammunition simply for testing purposes. That struck the Auditor General, and it would strike anybody else in the same way. The Auditor General goes on:
I have reason to believe that the ammunition was resold at an advance of about 25 per cent, and that its destination was not Vickers, Limited. I may be mistaken in this, but Colonel Allison's connection with the transaction does not tend to allay suspicion. I wrote the Department .of Militia and Defence, asking to be furnished with an Order in Council, etc, etc.
I repeat what the Auditor General says here, that there is reason to believe that the ammunition was sold at an advance of about 25 per cent. He does not say to whom, but I think I am warranted in saying that there is strong reason for believing that the ammunition was sold to the Imperial authorities, and I say this upon the statement made by the Minister of Militia and Defence himself. On page 7 of this file is found the following statement by the Minister of Militia and Defence:
Re the sale of defective ammunition. The Canadian Treasury has received $20 for every thousand rounds thereof. There are no records available to show what became of it, further than that it was regularly ordered and shipped to Vickers, one of the most reputable firms in the world. The assurance was given that not

one cent was paid in commission by the firm to any one, and no profit was made on it. It
is understood-
These words are very vague.

It is understood that to cover the cost of transport, handling-, exchange, insurance, etc.j a sum was added by one cf V'ckers' officers to the price, but on learning that these expenses were borne by the British Government they were immediately removed.
These expenses were borne by the British Government. What is the meaning of that? If the ammunition was consumed by Vickers themselves, there was no necessity for adding to the price. If they were selling it to somebody else, then of course it was necessary to add to the price the cost of transport, handling, exchange, insurance, etc. Mark the closing words of this paragraph, and I leave it to the sense of any man to say whether they do not furnish irrefutable evidence that the purchaser from Vickers, Limited, was the Imperial authorities. Why were the expenses to be bt)rne by the British Government unless the ammunition was sold to -the British Government? And this is from the report of the Minister of Militia and Defence himself. The Minister of Militia and Defence also states:
The Canadian Treasury has received $20 for every thousand rounds thereof. There are no records available to show what became of it.
And he ends the paragraph thus:
On learning that these expenses were borne by the British Government they were immediately removed.
It seems to me that he knows more than he pretends to know; that he knows this ammunition, after it was sold by him to Vickers, Limited, was sold by them-or at all events through the agency of Colonel Allison-to the Imperial authorities. That is something which I say is absolutely inexcusable. Will anybody in this country excuse the Minister of Militia or the Government for having depleted our stock of ammunition by selling this quantity to Vickers, Limited, and allowing them to sell it at a profit to the Imperial authorities. That is the charge which is made to-day; that is the charge which is borne out by the record, and it is that for which we ask an investigation. I repeat what I said a moment ago: the Prime Minister, not upon one occasion only, but on occasions almost without number during the present session has stated that if a charge were made against one of his colleagues or against the Government, nothing would be allowed to stand 246
in the way of an investigation. The Minister of Militia himself has repeated more than once that he desires the most ample investi-tion. The defence made to-day by the Prime Minister is that the matter has been referred to the Davidson Commission. I have to complain of one thing, and it is this:	We should have had this OrdeT in
Council brought before us to-day, and long before to-day; it should have been laid upon the Table as- soon as it was passed. The House has a right to be informed whenever a matter of this kind is referred to a commission to be investigated, so that the men who had called the attention of the Government to the matter might have an opportunity of following the inquiry. The charge which I make to-day is that the Government is not giving to this charge the most ample investigation.
There are two investigating commissions sitting in Ottawa to-day. Will any one pretend that the Davidson Commission will give the same degree of satisfaction to the public as the Commission presided over by Sir William Meredith and Mr. Justice Duff? Will any one pretend that it is possible to expect that this matter will be probed to the bottom-investigated out and out- before the Davidson Commission as it would be before the Commission presided over by Sir William Meredith and Mr. Justice Duff? How are the two commissions composed? One is composed of a single judge, and the other is composed of two judges. The Davidson Commission, composed of a single judge, has no counsel to prosecute this charge before the commissioner. There is only one young man, eminent in his profession, I admit, to assist the commissioner. But I have this to say against Mr. Thompson's investigating this matter. If I am correctly informed, Mr. Thompson, who assists the commissioner, is an officer in the Militia, under the Minister of Militia and Defence. Will niy right hon. friend or any other hon. gentleman tell me that it is proper that the Minister of Militia should be investigated by a commissioner who is assisted by one of the officers of the Minister of Militia? If we are to have an investigation the ordinary rules should be . followed. On the other hand, there is before the Commission presided over by Sir William Meredith and Mr. Justice Duff, a counsel appointed to represent the Opposition. Have they not the same Tight to investigate one charge as to investigate another? If the Government thought they owed it to the country, under the



existing circumstances in which we are placed, that the fuse charges should be so probed that the country could have absolute faith and confidence in the Tesult, and that the Opposition should be allowed to select a counsel so that both sides of the case would be represented and the fullest probing of the matter ensured, is there not as much reason why this matter should also be investigated in the same manner by the same commission? The only reason given by my right hon. friend why the matter was placed in the hands of the Davidson Commission was because certain witnesses were at present available in Ottawa. Those witnesses can always be procured whenever they are needed, and if the investigation cannot take place immediately because other matter are being investigated at present, it can be delayed for a few weeks, so that his reason is not a valid one why the course I have suggested should not be taken. My right hon. friend is not living up to-day to the pledge which he has boastingly given on more than one occasion that upon any charges there will be a full investigation. The investigation before the Davidson Commission is not a full investigation; it is not satisfactory, and we must press to have the matter referred to the Meredith-Duff Commission.
Sir SAM HUGHES (Minister of Militia and Defencef: Mr. Speaker, Let me say at the outset that I am delighted to see the right hon. leader of the Opposition in such good form. From what I have heard recently, I expected that he would come here in an ambulance and be attended by two or three nurses. I understand he has recently been passing through a very trying time; that he has been passing through political tribulations.
He is feeling pretty good.

His voice had little of the ring that I used to hear in it in 1896, when his hair was Longer than it is to-day and hardly so gray, when he used to tell the people of Ontario: Hands off Manitoba, and when he would go down to Quebec and say to the people there: Trust me, a Frenchman and a Roman Catholic and shun Tupper, who is an Englishman and a Protestant. His voice had somewhat of the pathos of the olden times but hardly the

ring in it. I understood that the House was not sitting on Saturdays, and I thought the right hon. gentleman was going to take the opportunity of doing some recruiting.

Recruiting is going on excelltently, but in the place where the right hon. leader of the Opposition might exercise some influence, I am sorry to say that it needs a little stimulant, and I trust Tie will direct his attention to that matter and make use of that pathos that he has exhibited here to-day.
5 p.m. He has complained that Captain Thompson, a lawyer, is engaged before Sir Charles Davidson. The fact that Captain Thompson wears the uniform of a British ofiicer is a good reason why he should be regarded as entirely worthy to appear before Sir Charles Davidson, and it is one of the surest guarantees that he is an jionest man. I have not, however, the slightest doubt that from the great array of legal talent behind the right hon. leader of the Opposition he can select suitable counsel, in case Captain Thompson cannot find time to attend to the duties of the court, to take his place. I do not find as many of my right hon. friends in uniform as I would like to find.
I will briefly analyse this matter. The charge was made before I arrived here that the price of this ammunition was too low. I may say that it is exactly the cost of the ammunition and it is just twice the price that was offered a year or so ago for the same ammunition. The statement was made that it was not known where the ammunition was going. The correspondence brought down clearly shows that it' was ordered by the firm of Vickers-Maxim, one of the most reputable firms in the world, and was shipped to them, and that the money was paid by them to the Bank of Montreal in England. The statement was made that the ammunition was resold. That statement is absolutely untrue. The ammunition was sold to Vickers-Maxim and the address given of one of their officers. The statement was made that no Order in Council was passed.

There was no necessity for an Order in Council in regard to the matter. According to the law, the quartermaster general could have thrown the ammunition into the river St. Lawrence. That is with reference to that made 'before 1909, and subsequent to 1909 the officer commanding the district of Quebec had the absolute authority to destroy ammunition on an order from General Macdonald, that is, on an order from a " superior authority." General Macdonald, on receiving the intimation to sell the ammunition, did not consider that to be " superior authority," and he therefore came and got me to initial the document. The reason I asked for an Order in Council in regard to the 2,000,000 rounds was because the quantity was so large that I thought the responsibility, if anything transpired, should be divided. The cost price of the ammunition, when it was supposed to be in good condition, was $20 per thousand. I have not heard of any price of $34.60, and I do not know what that refers to. Mark VI ammunition is not being manufactured to-day in any part of the British Empire, and, therefore, there is no need to refer at all to that particular ' size. The statement was made that the ammunition was illegally sold. As it was sold under the regulations of the department, the sale was a perfectly legal one. The statement was made that there was a shortage of ammunition. After- the war broke out there was a shortage of good ammunition because we sent it all to the front, but I sent an order to the quartermaster general to replenish the store of good ammunition according to the requirements of the country at that time, until we would have a sufficient store of Mark VI ammunition. I also directed that the best of the Mark VI ammunition should be returned, but in order to get it out of the way the Militia Council decided that we had better destroy the 12,000,000 rounds ordered to be destroyed by the Barlow Commission a year before, in order to prevent any portion of it getting mixed up with other ammunition, and that the Mark VI ammunition manufactured up to the time of the Barlow Commission, which ammunition was declared to be defective, should be retained in case of an emergency in this country before we could get Mark VII ammunition manufactured in sufficient quantities.
Long before I became Minister of Militia it was known that the ammunition being manufactured in the Dominion Arsenal was
defective; every rifleman in Canada knew that, and report after report brought forth only the statement: Oh, you do not understand the matter, and so forth. I remember on one occasion, after I became minister, going through the factory and putting my hand on one of the machines. I caught five or six cases as they came out, and out of five cases three were defective, as could be seen with the naked eye. The machines needed trueing up. But to any suggestion made about possible improvements, we were told that we didn't understand it and that the best possible was being done. We could buy the English ammunition which would not give any blow-backs, but in the case of our own ammunition, about six rounds out of ten would show a blow-back-that is the powder would be blown back through the cap-hole, or at the point where the case was defective, permitting the discharge from the breech instead of from the muzzle. Therefore, soon after becoming minister, I consulted the Prime Minister and we obtained authority to issue a commission to inquire into the manufacture of ammunition in the Dominion arsenal. We communicated with the British War Office, and they sent to us two of the greatest experts on these subjects, Colonel Sir H. Barlow, and Major Ogilvie. These gentlemen came here and made a very minute inspection of the Dominion arsenal. A summary of that report has been presented to the House by the Prime Minister. Twelve million rounds of ammunition made prior to 1908 were rejected on account of cracked cases and other defects, and were ordered to be destroyed. The suggestion was made that the bullet should be taken out of them, and so on. The balance of the ammunition was declared to be "under suspicion." In other words, the whole of the ammunition was declared to be defective-twelve million rounds made prior to 1908 ordered to be destroyed, and the balance manufactured up to 1913 declared to be " under suspicion and defective." That " under suspicion and defective " ammunition, I venture to say, could not be used in the Mark II Boss or Lee-Enfield rifle, with safety. But I will not go into that aspect of the case unless it is deemed necessary. We did what we could to prevent these blow-backs and render the ammunition more or less efficient, by putting it to a process which we call " ringing." One of the officers in the arsenal thought that by putting each cartridge in a slot and pressing the metal at

Yes, the explosive blowing-hack in the face of the soldier. We are paying pensions now to some such cases, while others were injured and laid up for a long time. So, it was found that this " ringing" did not remove the trouble. Accordingly, the ammunition declared by the Barlow report to be defective ammunition made subsequent to 1908, was set aside as fit for machine gun use only. But when it came to the big camp at Valcartier in 1914, the British Government, wishing to get every round of good ammunition that was possible, and desiring that all our ammunition made subsequent to 1913 should be shipped to the front, we did ship it. We gave our boys a chance to practice by using the Mark III Ross rifle, which is much more powerful than the Mark II, and we used for rifle practice this Mark VI ammunition, the ranges being short. We inspected it carefully and used the best we could find. Even then, as the camp drew to a close, the men found that the ammunition was not right, that it was defective owing to blow-backs, explosions, detonations, and so on, and they were getting nervous over the use of it. Therefore, we held it up.
Just before the troops sailed from Quebec, on my return from Gaspe Basin, we held a council and talked over the supply of ammunition. We were deficient in ammunition at that time-it is no harm to admit it now, when our supply is ample. We decided to get rid of that manufactured before 1908 and1 keep the balance of the Mark VI ammunition in hand in case of an emergency. If the worst came to the worst we would use it. The Quartermaster General, as explained in his report, has steadily built up a proper store of Mark VTI ammunition. I gave this order before I sailed for England. The deputy minister, the Master General of the Ordnance, the Quartermaster General and the Chief of the General Staff, each disseminated it to his officers, the object being to hold the ammunition in case of an emergency, and that is the reason of these orders appearing on the papers. In England I heard stories that a number of the

soldiers had suffered at Valcartier, having blow-backs in the use of the ammunition. Once a man has a blow-back it renders him nervous in firing any rifle. A good deal of that kind of thing had occurred at Valcartier, and a number of the fellows were more or less nervous over this ammunition. Accordingly, on my return, it was decided that none of this Mark VI ammunition should be used. And the store of Mark VII was gradually coming up to the full height, and I am happy to say that it has long since passed the high water-mark of what is necessary for the defence of the country. The Mark VI ammunition was lying in store, the order of the board being that it was to be used only for machine gun testing. We have no machine guns to test, ours being tested before we receive them. This order became known to the ammunition men throughout the country, and there were requests for the ammunition. One was received, but was not fulfilled, as we did not know where the ammunition was going-something was said of its going to Mexico. In another case, I was willing that it should be allowed to go. It was sold, not in large quantities, but in small quantities here and there.
There is a misunderstanding as to Mark VII ammunition, which I might as well clear up at this time. The Mark VII is much more elaborately made than the Mark VI. It has a more pointed tip, the point being filled with aluminum inside, backed up with lead to preserve the balance of the bullet in its course. It is one thirty-third inch longer than the Mark VI. When we use Mark VII ammunition in the Mark II rifle, which is the old Ross rifle, the sharper point of the bullet sometimes prevents the ready entrance of the cartridge into the barrel. Therefore, the word was passed without any undue ceremony that in using Mark VII ammunition in the Mark II rifle it was well not to use the rifle as a magazine rifle'but as a singleloader; and with green troops this is much better.
As regards the sale of this ammunition, I was spoken to about it by a representative of the Vickers firm who was then in Canada-one of the firm. The question came up of the making of ammunition in Canada, and when I told him that I understood that the British Government had ample facilities for making ammunition, the question came up whether we could spare what was understood to be defective ammunition, for testing machine guns or something of that kind. The whole con-

versation did not occupy hall a minute. My answer to him was to communicate with General Macdonald, Quartermaster-General, who had the matter in charge. There was another conversation some time later, not with this distinguished gentleman, but with one who, at one time, was a good friend of the right hon. leader of the Opposition, Colonel J. Wesley Allison.
Oh, oh.

speechtext:
But if it suits the right hon. member's policy

'
Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
If it is the policy of the Tight hon. member to play executioner in respect to the gentlemen who sit around him-half of them sit here to-day dreading the block-let me assure him that that is not the policy that this individual pursues towards his friends. Until I find
that they have proved traitor to me I do not go back on them, as was the case with regard to a number of gentlemen who sat behind the right hon. leader of the Opposition in the days gone by in the House of Commons of Canada. I am glad to see fire in the right hon. member's eye at this moment; I will light him up a little more if he wishes it.
This ammunition was first ordered, I say, by the members of the Vickers firm. Finally it was ordered by Col. J. Wesley Allison, who has the honour of being the Vickers representative, and who had, and still has, the honour of having been selected; by the special representative of the British; Government as agent in the United States-of America in respect of very large matters-' of international concern. He is 'a gentleman who to-day stands high in the estimation of the people of the country, not from fear-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Not from fear, not from trembling, not from having a solid phalanx behind his back -and, to keep it there, playing one role in one part of Canada and the old English school philosopher in the other. He holds the good opinion of this House and this country to-day, and he holds it by merit. This gentleman ordered the ammunition. He saw the Quartermaster General, and the Quartermaster General consulted me. The Quartermaster General knows his business-I never yet found him wrong on a legal point-so I put my initial on his memorandum and the ammunition was shipped to Vickers in London. The money was paid to the Bank of Montreal, and a straighter transaction never was conducted in this Dominion of Canada. I did not know how much of this ammunition they would want, for they were getting thousands of these machine guns. However, our first desire was- that the soldiers going to the front should not be obliged to use one round of defective ammunition; that they should get the very best that could be obtained. By securing the release of a few million rounds of good ammunition from Britain that would otherwise have been used for the machine guns- and it was pointed out in a report read by the Prime Minister that this ammunition was capable of being used for that purpose -by securing this release, I say, through letting the Vickers people have this defective ammunition, I claim that we were doing the country a service. By the way,

the right hon. gentleman forgot to talk about the retreat from Mons to the Marne. Surely he could have shown that this sale of ammunition compelled the British to retreat to the Marne-that is another of his fads that he generally makes use of. By releasing this ammunition we did the British Empire a good service, and benefited the Canadian treasury by bringing back $20 for every thousand rounds of ammunition.
The right hon. member dilates upon the argument about keeping that ammunition in store. I want to tell him that so long as I am Minister of Militia-and I intend to be Minister of Militia until I go out-I assume my full responsibility and intend to exercise it. So long as I am Minister of Militia, not one round of that defective ammunition will be given to any of our soldiers by me or by my authority to fire at the enemy. When our men go into action we want them to go with the very best materials, the very best equipment, the very best ammunition that can be got. I purpose at a very early date ascertaining where this defective ammunition is and settling the matter once for all by getting rid of it, in a legitimate way. If we do that, then the defective ammunition will be entirely out of the way; it will no longer take up storage room, and good ammunition will be served to the boys so that they shall be able to perform their duties. Not one round of this ammunition is held by me for defensive purposes. For that we have no warrant or authority.
The hon. member quotes from the Auditor 'General. And the Auditor General oocupies a peculiar position; it is hardly proper for any member of Parliament to stand up here and criticise him. But when the Auditor General undertakes to say what he has said in the document which has been read; when he makes reflection upon a gentleman who has more honour in his little finger than the Auditor General has in his whole carcass, I want to tell him that I will find some means of reaching the Auditor General. I will permit no man occupying the position of public servant in this country, so far as I am concerned, whether in office or out of office, so to misconduct himself as to pen the letter which he has penned-I never saw it until to-day-to the Minister of Finance. Had such a letter been sent to me-indeed, I did get one of a somewhat similar character, and it was dealt with in double quick time-had such a letter as that come from the Auditor General to the Minister

of Militia, it would have been returned in mighty short metre with an intimation that the writer had better study his duties and learn to pen his letters in proper form.
The right hon. member asks why this ammunition was not sold direct to the British Government instead of to the Vickers' Company. I do not see what the British Government knew about it. We sold them all the good ammunition we could spare early in the war. This ammunition was asked for; we realised that the use of it would be a good way to test the machine guns, and it went. The story was that this ammunition was being Tesold by Vickers for the machine gun purposes of the British Admiralty and that Vickers were making $5 per thousand rounds on it. Well, if Vickers paid the freight, insurance and exchange charges on that ammunition, which were pretty heavy at that time, then they would not be any money in pocket by turning it over to the Admiralty at $25, when they paid $20 for it. I do not know anything about it, only this: When I was in England, having heard the yarn, I asked one of the Vickers' officers-I think it was Mr. Searles-about the matter. He said he did not know the details of it, but that he had heard these stories. He said they had added this sum to the cost, but as soon as they found that the Admiralty would themselves meet the cost, they wiped out the one pound sterling that had: been added and the price stood at the $20 that the Government charged them for the ammunition and for sending it over.
Let me summarize. All ammunition made before 1913 and in store was condemned as defective by the commission. All of the defective ammunition made prior to 1909 was condemned to destruction in one form or another. The balance was recommended for machine gun practice only. However, in order to have as little of this destroyed as possible, we decided to use that recommended to be used in machine gun practice or. in Mark III rifles. We tried it out quietly, after ringing it as I have described; and decided to use it, not in Mark II or Lee-Enfield, but in Mark III Roes rifles. Ringing it, however, was found not to benefit the defective ammunition to any great extent, and in some cases it injured it. There were several proposals for the sale of defective ammunition. One was made by the deputy minister at $10 or $12.50, supposedly for Mexico. Another was to sell to Vickers, through their New York agent, Allison, for machine gun testing. This was for 2,000,000 rounds at

$20-that is an error in my notes, apparently, as it should be 3,000,000 rounds at $20.
The Quartermaster-General, following the usual practice in Canada regarding condemned military material, authorized the sale, and obtained the endorsation of the minister in addition. I again point out that when cases of this kind arise in a district, the district officer commanding, if he feels that he wants any superior author

ity to dispose of condemned material, looks to the Quartermaster-General for that superior authority. As a rule it is considered, and has been so acted upon, that the Quartermaster-General's authority is sufficient, In destroying one and a half million rounds at Winnipeg the Quartermaster-general was regarded as the superior authority; but General Macdonald did not wish to regard himself as the superior authority in time of war, so he came to me and asked me to place my initials on the order, which I gladly did. The goods were then regularly shipped to an officer in the Vickers' works in England, Mr. Searles. There was no commission paid, offered or asked by anyone in the transaction. That was brought out this morning before the Davidson Commission. We got $20, and that was all that was paid for the ammunition, so that there could not be any commission. The quartermaster general had the money placed directly to the credit of the Receiver General of Canada. ;Thus it passed through no one's hands.
This defective ammunition released a similar quantity of good English ammunition for the front. It has 'been asserted that Vickers' officer in England added, for transport, freight, insurance, exchange, handling and risk, one pound sterling additional, and then -sold the lot to the British Admiralty for $25 per thousand. The Militia Department has no Tecord of this, the sale 'being direct to Vickers' officer, Mr. Searles, in England. All we know is the insinuation in the Auditor General's Report and remarks heard in various places throughout this country. The sale was made direct to Vickers' officer. Mr. Searles, in England. But I am informed, on good authority, that on finding all expenses were paid by the Admiralty, Mr. Searles withdrew the charge of $5. This, however, is a matter entirely between Mr. Searles and the Admiralty; it is a matter with which this department has nothing whatever to do. This ammunition, or any of the defective ammunition, was
ordered to toe held in store by the minister in 1914, and ordered further not to be used in Mark II rifle in any circumstances. The part that I ordered to be destroyed in 1914 was the part made prior to 1909, which was ordered not to be used on any consideration.
The net result is that, by the sale of the
2.000.	000 rounds of defective ammunition referred to, Canada has received $40,000 which would never have been received;
2.000.	000 of good English ammunition has been released for the front; an ample store of good new Mark VII ammunition is held in store for use in Canada. It is now universally recognized that Mark VII, new and good ammunition, can be used in Mark II rifles, while the condemned Mark VI should not be used, and has been forbidden. Under no circumstances would the ammunition sold be allowed to be used in Mark II Titles, the one retained for arming the troops in Canada. The balance of the defective ammunition could not be used in either Mark II Ross rifle or Lee-Enfield rifle. It cannot be safely used even in Mark III rifle, even for practice. The practice in England is to treat such matters as the QuartermiasterMGeneral has treated this sale of condemned material.
I may say that, while in England, I made inquiries about this and found that such a transaction would never reach the Quartermaster-General, much less the minister, and certainly never the Cabinet. The practice is that the officer commanding in the district calls his board and the board makes a report. The officer commanding then orders the ammunition disposed of as condemned, and places any money received to the credit of the Government in the official way. Thus in every sense we have been well within our rights in the Militia Department in dealing with this matter as we have done.
I have to say, in conclusion, that no Canadian soldier will, so long as I am Minister of Militia, be requested or permitted, if we know it, to carry one round of this condemned mark VI ammunition in his pouch for service in action. When our boys go into action we want them to feel as confident as it is possible for men to feel. Napoleon asserted that the sentimental as against the material is as three to one in fighting; and if you have men poorly armed, poorly equipped, using bad ammunition, that sentimental diminishes to nothing, and you lose three-fourths of your fighting power. I want my boys to go in

feeling they have the best rifle in the world, the best ammunition in the world, and that they can handle themselves in a manner to equal the best.

Mr. Speaker, the somewhat wonderful statement of the Minister of Militia reminds me of a quotation from the Bible which I think I can quote correctly: " The wicked flee when no man pursueth." I would like to know who ever asked the Minister of Militia to send our boys to the front with defective ammunition. I would like to know what a discussion about giving J. Wesley Allison a rake-off of $5,000 has to do with sending our boys to the front with poor ammunition. I want to answer the minister in a logical, fair manner, but it is pretty bard to do so, after listening to the arguments he has used. This is not a question of whether or not there was bad ammunition in Canada. If the Government bad1 poor ammunition or defective ammunition on their hands, this country has money enough to take charge of that and to throw it into the river, if necessary, and get good ammunition in its place. The question which we are bringing up here to-day, which was first brought up by the Auditor General-and I think, notwithstanding the dire threats made by the Minister of Militia, that once in a while it is a good thing for Canada that there is an Auditor General. The question brought up by him is the fact that defective ammunition was owned by the Dominion of Canada; that the Minister of Militia, through his counsellor, friend and guide, J. Wesley Allison, sold this, not to Vickers, but through Vickers, to the British Admiralty, at a rake-off of $5 a thousand rounds.
