We must have a great deal less respect for the Prime Minister and his colleagues than we had before that, because I want to tell the Prime Minister that it does him and his colleagues very little credit that in a matter of .this importance they should select the commissioner who has on previous occasions been chosen by the Minister of Militia in order to investigate things which have turned out so rotten that the name of Canada is a disgrace ' and a by-word among the civilized nations of the world.
iSir SAM HUGHES: Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that I have chosen Sir Charles Davidson?
I mean what I say.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman does not care to repeat what he said I am not particular; I pay no attention to what he 6ays anyway.

I am not going to repeat; hut what I said I stand by. I tell the Premier that if he thinks he can satisfy the people of Canada by referring matters of this importance to Sir Charles Davidson, in the light of what this commission had done during the last year, he is living in a fool's paradise. The people of this country will not stand for any more hiding and covering up of the'dishonest and nefarious
(Mr. Carvell.]
transactions of my right hon. friend's friends and supporters. There is no use trying to hide the thing or smooth it over. We have had enough illustrations in the last few months of the attitude of the Premier, and we might as well just come out and call a spade a spade, as Sir William Meredith said at the commission the other day. Day after day and week after week since this Parliament assembled in January last, we have sought for an opportunity to get the light of day on many transactions of the friends of this Government, and* we have been balked at every turn except in one case where the Government were driven to it by a power whose name I am not at liberty to mention in this House. They have refused us investigations, and have made one flimsy excuse after another, and when driven from one citadel to another-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What does the hon. member mean when he says we were driven to a course of action by a power he is not at liberty to mention?
I mean exactly what I say.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If I understand the inference, I want to say that that statement is absolutely devoid of the slightest semblance of truth.
I am glad I am getting my right hon. friend interested; that was my object in speaking this afternoon.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am glad you are pleased.

They have refused investigations of things which any reasonable intelligent man knows are so dishonest that they would stink in the nostrils of every man in Canada. They have refused to extend the scope of investigations because they dare not, on account of what would happen to their friends. They have * handed this matter over to a commission appointed more .than a year ago, when perhaps my right hon. friend was sincerely penitent for some things that had been revealed in the Public Accounts Committee, and at that time he said that the doors of the penitentiary were yawning for those who sold lame and decrepit horses to the British Government, and for those who boodled in bandages, boots and binoculars, and everything else they could get their hands on that was required for the army during the nation's stress. I want to tell my right hon. friend that these doors are still yawning, and unless there is greater

i 3911
activity on the part of my right hon. friend and his Government than there has been in the past, the doors will still remain yawning for his friends who have been guilty of looting the public treasury. If my right hon. friend can take any comfort out of the course he has pursued during the last year and the results of the investigation of his special commissioner, Sir Charles Davidson, he is welcome to it. I am not here to attack Sir Charles Davidson personally, and what I have to say about him as a commissioner I want to say right here in the public light of Parliament. A gentleman who has occupied the high position that this man has, a gentleman who for nearly a year has been investigating such things as the Government would allow him to investigate, a gentleman who, so far as we can judge, concluded his labours three months ago, with the exception of one small transaction, a gentleman who has not the honesty-I think I may use the word-to bring down to Parliament after we had been in session for three or four months, a report on' matters so important as he has been charged to investigate-such a man is not the one to whom the people of Canada want to have referred important matters with which the Minister of Militia is concerned. I say that to my right ihon. friend with a full sense of the responsibility for what I am saying. A gentleman who has investigated the nefarious horse deals in Nova Scotia and driven one member of Parliament of that province out of public life, a gentleman who has investigated other nefarious horse deals in the province of Ontario and driven out of public life a member of the Ontario Legislature, a gentleman who has investigated the bandage and drug transactions here in the city of Ottawa, which, I was told early in the session, had driven another member of Parliament out of public life, a gentleman who has investigated all these things and will not make his report on them to Parliament either is not fit .for the position he occupies or he is holding back the report at the instigation of the men who appointed him. I do not care which horn of the dilemma my .hon. friends choose. I have tried to state my position in language as plain as I could use, and I think I have the ability of using fairly plain language when the occasion requires. I want to tell my hon. friends that if they think they can cover up their tracks and whitewash and cleanse the character of the Minister of Militia and Defence by hand-'
ing these nefarious and dirty transactions over to the Davidson Commission, they are making the greatest mistake they ever made.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: As the hon. gentleman has mentioned character, let mb point out that I have never been caught impersonating people in New York or buying blackguards to steal papers from New York offices.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Militia is welcome to all the pleasure he gets out of this. He will get his answer, probably before many days are gone by.
If there were no dirty papers, they could not be stolen.

I tell him right here
that he cannot draw the attention of the people of Canada away from the doings of his friend Allison, and his portion of the divvy of half a million dollars, by throwing dust in the people's eyes about anybody trying to steal papers. Don't let the Minister of Militia deceive himself on that point. Don't let him feel that he can help his cause or protect a man who has practically pilfered a quarter of a million dollars from the people of Canada, by throwing out any nasty insinuations about what I or any other member of Parliament may have done in New York or elsewhere. Neither he nor his friend Allison, nor the Ottawa Free Press, the champion and organ of his friend Allison, can get the people of Canada to forget the real question by any such smallbore tactics as that.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

It will take me only a few moments to conclude the remarks that I want to address to the House. Before I refer to the subject matter under discussion I wish very shortly to refer to a most uncalled for and insulting remark made by the Minister of Militia just before the House rose at six o'clock with reference to my taking papers from some source unknown, and from which I had no right to take them. In making that remark he followed up a course of conduct which he, his counsel, and a friendly newspaper have been carrying on for the last three or four days. I want to assure my hon. friend that shortly after the Meredith-Duff Commission was created I took every reasonable means in my power of obtaining information as to the conduct of himself and of his friend,

counsellor, and guide, Colonel Allison. In doing so I found it necessary to go to the city of New York and other places in the United States. I had not been very long on the ' investigation when I became well satisfied that my hon. friend the minister was attempting to put up a very nice job on me for the purpose of drawing public attention away from his own conduct, and that of hiis friend and his Mend's friends. I therefore employed, as my solicitor and counsel in the city of New York, William Travers Jerome. I consulted two other men of such prominence that when their names are made public, even my hon. friend the minister will have no doubt of the wisdom of my course, and I consulted no man, discussed no plan and made no move without first consulting one of the three gentlemen to whom I have referred, my solicitor having been named. I want to tell the minister that when the reports of the detectives which have been furnished to me toy Mr. Jerome are made public, as they will toe, if and when necessary, he will not make any nasty insinuations about my trying to obtain papers to which I have no right. I want to say further that during the last four months I have been in only two legal offices in the city of New York, one being that of William Travers Jerome, and the other that of Kiddle and Margison, of 115 Broadway, on the 14th floor. My friends are at liberty to investigate those two firms as much as they like. So far as any firms of German name are concerned, I know nothing about them; I have never seen them, and I have had no correspondence nor communication with them. Whenever my hon. friend the minister wants to pursue this case any further before the tribunal having jurisdiction over it, I am ready to meet him and give him all the information whidb he desires, and I hope that before I am through with him I shall give him a little more than he would like to have made public.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: My hon. friend has stated that I put up a plant on him. The plant was put up toy the hon. member himself and his friends, as I am prepared to show. The first news which I had when I reached New York city was the intimation of the plant which this gentleman has put up with a certain gentleman to whom I have referred.

I am not going to discuss this question with the minister further except to say to him that I had not

been in the city of New York for more than a year until at least a week after the mihister returned from England. I have nothing further to say as to this, but I do not want the Minister of Militia to attempt to cover his dirty tracks by attempting to throw dirt at me.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The Minister of
Militia is prepared to face this hon. gentleman in this House or before any other tribunal in the world. Let me assure the hon. member that when the matter is all cleared up, the Minister of Militia will have no cause to blush for any of his actions and if the hon. gentleman does not blush, it will be because he has a rhinoceros hide on him.

I want briefly to refer
to the question before the House. The right hon. leader of the House has attempted to show that this transaction was all right, because, he says, they got more than the ammunition was worth. If my right hon. friend can take any satisfaction or glorification out of selling through the agency of Col. John Wesley Allison condemned ammunition to the British Admiralty for twice as much as it is worth, he is quite at liberty to do so, and if his friends in this House can take any comfort out of that, so far as I am concerned, they are welcome to it. That is the question. The question is not whether the ammunition was worth $20 a thousand or $10 a thousand or $12.50 a thousand. There is no use in my friend's or my friend's friends trying to get away from the real question. While I do not make the statement, I do say that I am informed on the best possible authority- and if anything like a fair investigation is given, it can easily be proved-that the reason sent up to the Council when this matter was first brought before it, was that this was condemned ammunition and not to be used for testing purposes, ana when it was pointed out that they would never be able to pass an Order in Council to sell condemned ammunition to the British Admiralty, the reason was changed and put in the form that the ammunition was being sold for testing purposes.
Sir ROBERT BORDEN. I do not quite understand the point my hon. friend is making. Does he say that there was a recommendation to Council to sell this ammunition to the British Admiralty?

I am informed that when this matter first came before the Council, it was put on the plea or argument that this

was condemned ammunition sold to the British Admiralty or the British Government and that accounted for the reduction in the price.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
For the third
time, I affirm that the statement made by my hon. friend to the House just now is without the shadow of any foundation whatever.

The next question is:
How are you going to investigate? If this thing is bad enough to require an investi-tion of any kind, then it requires and demands a genuine investigation. If it does not require and demand a genuine investigation, then my right hon. friend is not fair to the Minister of Militia and Defence.
My right hon. friend is pillorying Sir Sam Hughes before the people of this country as being charged with doing that which he ought not to do. I repeat again-either this is of sufficient importance to be investigated, or else it should be left alone; it is too serious a matter to trifle with, too serious to play the petty game of politics with.
Oh, oh.

One hon. gentleman
says:	We are investigating it. You are
investigating it by the Davidson Commission. I am not going to spend much more time on the Davidson Commission. It is the greatest farce my right hon. friend the Prime Minister has created in his-four years of farcical government. At the head of it is a man who, as I said this afternoon-I do not know whether it is because he has not the ability, or because he has not the conscience, or because he is acting under dictation-has laboured for a year, has squandered about $20,000 of the public money of Canada, and has brought forth nothing in the way of a report, and nothing to justify his existence. If I had any desire to exercise any influence with Sir Charles Davidson, I venture to say that it would have been an utterly useless undertaking on my part. Sir Charles Davidson was given an open commission. He was given a commission to investigate every matter connected with the expenditure of money by this Government for the purchase of arms or ammunition, of materials of any kind or description whatsoever for the purposes of this war. He was sent out with that open commission to investigate every charge, every insinuation that any one would be found to have the courage to come before that commission and make. That is all the instruction that he had, and that instruction has been, in spite of what the hon. gentleman says, carried out to the letter in a manner which has commanded the approbation of the public without distinction of party.
The hon. gentleman talked about investigations being burked. Well, it is a matter of public notoriety that that commission, everywhere it went, made its sittings public, and that it called on any one who had any charges to bring forth, any imputations to make, or any doubt to express as to whether something had not been wrongly done, to come forward and lay the. facts before that commission.
Something has been said about delay in the report. The report is not yet made; it is a considerable time since that commission was appointed. But is not an explanation, in large measure at least, to be found in the very thoroughness of that inquiry
and in its very wide scope? When the commission was named, comparatively few matters had been brought forward in respect of which the commission was called upon to decide. But as time went on, befqre those few matters were disposed of, other charges and insinuations were made, other matters were brought to the attention of the commission, with the result that during this period, during which we are told we have had no results, that commission has travelled from one ocean to the other, and has held investigations at every point in Canada where any man had one word to say, or any imputation whatsoever to make against any of the innumerable transactions which have been carried on by the Department of Militia during the course of this war. Is it to be wondered at that, having regard to the immense field of different charges and investigations that had to be covered, resulting in thousands of pages of testimony, we should not as yet have had a complete report? The hon. gentleman himself, who talks about this resultless commission, tells us that down in the Maritime Provinces it has sent one man out of public life; that right in this neighbourhood it has sent another man out of public life; that it has sent a man out of public life in the province of Ontario. I may tell him that it has sent a man in Regina behind the bars of the penitentiary, and has placed another man under surveillance waiting the decision of the American authorities in respect of extradition proceedings. The commission is spoken of as having been very useless, as having not yet reported. Surely these results are a testimony to the severity and the thoroughness with which the facts have been probed and inquired into by the commission. Since when are those, our sons and our brothers who have gone forth to risk, and, if need :be, to sacrifice MJieir lives in the defence of this country and of the Empire and of civilization, to be sneered at as the subordinates of the Minister of Militia? How will the people of Canada accept even from the right hon. gentleman the suggestion that When a man dons the uniform of an officer in His Majesty's service and goes forth, as I have said, to take his place with the men who are defending us and the liberties of this Empire, he forfeits his honour, his conscience, and his reliability, and that by that fact alone he becomes incompetent to act with regard, to investigations respecting the Militia Department, because, forsooth, he is the subordinate of the Minister of Militia? Surely hon. gentlemen are hard put to find a ground for insinuation against the honour, the integrity, the readiness and the. capacity to fearlessly and impartially perform his duty, of a man who, though he be young and in the eyes of the right hon. gentleman-that seems also to be a reproach to be made to 'him-has earned for himself an ehviable reputation for integrity and for ability in his profession, and a man who bears an inherited name that was in the lifetime of his father honoured, and that shall be honoured in this country as long as this country remains and keeps in mind the .memory of those men to whom she owes her greatest debt.
The hon. member for North Cape Breton may ask me now: " Why do yon gelt hot?" I would be ashamed of myself if I failed to get hot in the face of such an absolutely and unqualifiedly unworthy imputation-most assuredly unworthy of the right hon. gentleman, whether or not it be worthy of the hon. member for Carleton.
I have heard a great deal about motives in referring this matter to the Davidson Commission. Gentlemen have suggested, and we have heard .in addition to those imputations on the gentleman who is

acting as counsel for the people of Canada before that commission, other imputations. It has been suggested that there is some desire or intention to carry on the proceedings of that commission in secret. I have said that the proceedings of that commission from start to finish have been open to the public. They have been sitting in this building and have been sitting last week and have resumed their sittings this morning. The fact that they were so going to resume their sittings, and the subject they were going into were given out, as I am informed, to the press in the usual manner. My understanding was-I do not state that the thing was carried out because evidently the two hon. gentlemen who were sitting here did not have an intimation conveyed to them-that besides asking the Department of Militia to send everything that they had, besides suggesting that the Auditor General should be communicated with, I did say that the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) had asked a number of questions a day or two ago, and that I understood that the hon. member for South Cape Breton had contemplated making a motion, which at that time it was not intended to go on with. I suggested that they should be communicated with.
Perhaps the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) might not care to be associated with this matter, as he is not here. My constituency is North Cape Breton and Victoria.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Well, I suppose it is easier to keep cool in North Cape Breton than in South Cape Breton. My information is that endeavours were made to reach the hon. member for Pictou, and that they were not successful, and that with regard to the hon. member for North Cape Breton, what I had said apparently had not been understood, so that the accident did happen that the sitting opened this morning without these gentlemen having been communicated with. The Auditor General, however, was communicated with, and we must remember that upon thi-s record, so- far as it goes, the basis and source of any imputation that may be involved in the documents that are produced is the letter of the Auditor General. The Auditor General, as I have said, was communicated with, and interested himself in the gathering of information. Now, I am informed that the meeting this morning was really intended as a preliminary opening Qf the inquiry. It was held, as I understand it, in the usual place. Newspaper reporters, who had been informed of the fact yesterday or the day before, were present. The commission adjourned. It is to sit on Tuesday at ten o'clock in the morning in the same place. The witnesses that were heard this morning will all be there and all available for examination.
Will counsel be allowed?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am coming to that.
Since hon. gentlemen opposite are so anxious with regard to counsel in this particular matter, I am not disposed to make objections to counsel-being given. I am prepared to admit that this matter is on a different footing from matters of the nature of those that have -been investigated in the past, and abovie all, in view of the imputations which hon. gentlemen have seen proper to make upon the gentleman who occupies the position of adviser to the commission- whether he continues in that position or not is for him to decide after the conduct which we have witnessed this afternoon-if any hon. gentleman is prepared to assume the responsibility of such imputation or charge as may be contained in these papers and desires to be represented by counsel, I myself am quite ready to represent to the commissioner-I cannot undertake to control his action in the matter-that so far as I am concerned and this Government is concerned-and I am -satisfied I speak for the Minister of Militia as well as for every other member of the Government-there is not the slightest objection in the world to counsel appearing before the commission upon this particular matter.
In all the imputations which hon. gentlemen are so ready to make, I sometimes wonder whether we do not find verified in this House, on one side of it at least more perhaps than anywhere else, the truth of the saying that people are prone to judge others by themselves. In view, however, of the imputations that have been made, and to make it perfectly clear that, notwithstanding those imputations, there is in this Government absolutely no desire in the world other than that anything that can be given, by any possible construction, the face or appearance of a charge against this Government or any member of it, should have the most ample and thorough and competent investigation possible. I am free to say that, so far as this particular matter is concerned, and under the circumstances I have mentioned, if any hon. gentleman desires to assume the responsibility of those charges, there will be no objection to his having

counel to conduct such prosecution as he may be advised before the commission.

I do not wish to interrupt the hon. minister, but with his permission I desire to ask him a question. This commission of Sir Charles Davidson is appointed under the very same Act under which the Meredith-Duff Commission is appointed. In the Meredith-Duff Commission the Government agreed that the leader of, the Opposition should name counsel, and counsel was appointed. Now these are very important charges made by the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr McKenzie). Will the Government adopt the same course in this matter before Sir Charles Davidson as has been adopted in the Meredith-Duff Commission -arrange for the appointment of counsel and give that counsel the same status as counsel before the Meredith-Duff commission? If so, that would be an approach to reasonable fair play.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What I have said, perhaps, goes further than we said we would do with regard to the Duff-Meredith Commission. What was said with regard to the Duff-Meredith ' Commission was that the Government would appoint counsel to assist the Commissioners, and that the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier) should be at liberty to select one of these counsel. We have actually now counsel to assist the commission. I am going further; I am saying that if hon. gentlemen opposite take the responsibility of this charge .and want counsel to prosecute, for whatever purpose may run in their minds, we will be willing that they should have counsel before the commission.

The minister seems to be not quite fair. All I ask him is this. We have here two cases. The hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) made certain charges with regard to the purchase of fuses, and for that the Government appointed a commission under the Inquiries Act to make investigation. Now, the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie lias made certain charges with regard to the sale of ammunition. All I ask is that the Government should appoint counsel, having the same status exactly- neither more nor less-that Mr. Johnston has in the Meredith-Duff Commission. That is all we ask; will the minister do that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have used the words of the English language, as I understand them, which convey the idea that we are

willing that counsel should be appointed*. I do not know that I have anything more to say. I do not follow what it is I am asked to define.
Take away the condition you imply.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Do I understand that
what is asked is, when we are giving counsel to act for the people of Canada generally, hon. gentlemen opposite say: That is no good, we want counsel to act for somebody who is not the public of Canada? Surely that somebody else must be the somebody taking the responsibility of the charges.

The hon. member for
North Cape Breton is making the charges.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have said that there
' may be counsel before this commission to prove these charges the best he knows how. What further I can say I do not understand.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am done. I did not Tise to discuss the subject-matter of the so-called charge which the hon. member for North Cape Breton has made, and 1 have not gone into it. It is now before a competent tribunal of investigation, and 1 am absolutely satisfied to leave it there and to abide by the result which shall be reached. I rose only, I may say, because I felt that it was incumbent upon me, as a duty, not to let go unanswered such abso-. lutely reckless vilification-

I think that is out of
order, Mt. Speaker; the minister is forgetting himself.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext:
If the hon. minister
was referring to the words used by the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie, or by the hon. member for Carle-ton (Mr Carvell), I think he is out of order; but I understand that not to be the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think that under
your ruling, Mr. Speaker, I will have to admit that I was making that reference, and will have to withdraw the expression. The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugs-ley) suggested that I was forgetting myself. May I say that I was not forgetting myself that I was remembering the language of the hon. member for Carleton. However that language may be characterized, I felt that I should be doing very much less than my duty if I did not stand up to make-I do not know that I should call it a defence, because I am sure that the reputations of

the two gentlemen who have been attacked stand so high that they might be left to stand as the sole defence against the attack (I hope that is parliamentary) made upon them by the hon. member for Carleton. We had some discussion this afternoon on comparison of reputations. May I say to the hon. member for Carleton-and in this I am not depreciating in the slightest degree the height of his present reputation- that if he ever succeeds in attaining the reputation which Sir Charles Davidson has attained, after a long career lived out in the public eye, and under conditions in which his qualifications for such a position as he now occupies were put to the severest test, the hon. gentleman can flatter himself that his life has been that of one of the most honourable, the most distinguished of men whom Canada has produced.

Mr. Speaker, the matter now before the House may be said to be a sequel of what began as long ago as the 9th of March. The Minister of Justice charges my hon. friend from North Cape Breton with being in this position in bringing this matter before the House-that he desired to have something to talk about, having found that the Government had referred the matter to Sir Charles Davidson. The hon. minister should not have made that remark; it was totally unwarranted. It is just as well that we should be clear as to the facts. The hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie), on Monday last, informed the Prime Minister that he proposed to make a motion based on the papers that had been brought down. It was after my hon. friend from North Cape Breton had intimated that he would move in this matter that the Prime Minister moved.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I beg the hon.
gentleman's pardon. There is no foundation whatever for that statement.
Why not?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have already
explained, but the hon. member must have overlooked it, that on Thursday or Friday last I spoke to the Minister of Justice and told him that Sir Charles Davidson should be instructed to proceed with that inquiry. He saw Sir Charles Davidson on Saturday, I think. On Monday he reported to us that Sir Charles Davidson thought that an additional Order in Council would be necessary, and the recommendation was brought
to Council on Monday by the Minister of Justice.

It appears, then, that my right hon. friend discovered last Thursday that this was a matter that ought to be investigated. My- right hon. friend was very alow in bringing down information to the House in regard to this question. It took him two months to give to this House information which he might have given within two weeks after the matter was first called to his attention.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not think it was as long as that.
Mr. (MACDONALD: I will give the' House the story of the way in which this matter came before Parliament. Last Thursday it developed in the mind of -the Prime Minis' ter that this was a matter that ought to be investigated, and he communicated the fact to the Minister of Justice. He knew, or ought to have known when the idea first developed in his mind, that there was no power in Sir Charles Davidson, under the Order in Council under which he had been appointed a commissioner, to deal with this matter. My right hon. friend knew that last Thursday.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The statement that my hon. friend has just made is not a correct statement. It was not presented to my mind at all that -any further Order in Council would be necessary. That was first brought to my attention on Monday by the Minister of Justice.
Then my right hon. friend did not know the extent of the powers that he had previously conferred on Sir Charles Davidson?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did not have the Order in Council before me, and it did not occur to me that it related to purchase and did not include sale.

Why did my hon. friend not have in mind that according to the statement which he made to the House, and under the Order in Council creating the Meredith-Duff Commission he could have sent this matter to that commission without specially dealing with it? My right hon. friend intimated here more than once that the Order in Council creating the Meredith-Duff Commission contained powers which were sufficiently wide to enable him to send to that commission any matters coming up in Parliament that might require investigation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It would have required an Order in Council even in that case. My hon. friend ought to know that.

My right hon. friend some weeks ago constituted a commission which for the purposes of this discussion we will call the Meredith-Duff Commission. He announced and re-announced to the House that the Commission was constituted for the purpose of dealing not merely with those charges in which the name of J. Wesley Allison was mixed up, but with any other charges of a kindred nature that might arise. Some days after having brought down to the House the papers which, produced only a week ago Monday, he could have brought down long before that day, he decided that the papers which he himself had produced indicated the existence of a state of affairs which demanded an investigation. Instead of referring the matter to the commission which he had led the country to believe was constituted for the purpose of investigating matters relating to J. Wesley Allison, my right hon. friend in some inscrutable way decided to utilize the services of Sir Charles Davidson. Last Monday the member for North Cape Breton went to my right hon. friend and intimated to him that he purposed moving a resolution in the House based on the facts disclosed in the return brought down by the Prime Minister, and then and not till then did my right hon. friend disclose to the member for North Cape Breton the fact that he intended to refer .the matter to Judge Davidson. What did my right hon. friend do subsequent to that? On Tuesday the Order in Council was passed. He did not notify Parliament; he did not bring the Order in Council down to the House. No one in the country except my right hon. friend and his colleagues knew that such an Order in Council existed. It was his duty to give us the facts.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I beg my hon. friend's pardon. I have already stated that when the member for North Cape Breton spoke to me on Monday last I told him that the matter was referred to the Davidson Commission.
As a matter of fact, it had not been at that date.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The recommendation had been signed and sent to the Governor General for approval at the time that I made that statement to the hon. 
member for North Cape Breton and Victoria.

We have here in this file the memorandum of another Order in Council which had apparently been prepared but had never been approved or passed. It is rather curious, therefore, that my right hon. friend's Order in Council was in that position. But my right hon. friend has not told us why he failed to place on the table of the House the- Order in Council which was passed on Tuesday.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I told the hon. member for North Cape Breton that the matter had been referred to the Davidson Commission. If the Order in Council had been asked for, I should have been perfectly willing to lay it on the table of the House.
The Prime Minister does not say that he mentioned anything about an Order in Council to me?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I told my hon. friend that the matter had been referred.
There was no mention of an Order in Council.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It could only be referred by Order in Council of some kind.

My right hon. friend admits that he did not tell the member for North Cape Breton that an Order in Council had been passed. He simply used the word "referred," not the words "Order in Council." How could we ask for the Order in Council when we never knew it had been passed? It is a peculiar fact that though my right hon. friend mentioned to the member for North Cape Breton and Victoria the fact that the matter had been referred, the member for North Cape Breton and Victoria had no notice of that, and never knew that such an Order in Council had been passed. The memorandum of Council, which is like the one in the Militia Department of January 5, which was never passed, might never have been passed at all. My right hon. friend can find no good excuse in the assertion which he makes that if the Order in Council had been asked for he would have brought it down. My right hon. friend should have brought down the Order in Council, because no one but himself and a few of his colleagues knew that such a document existed. I think my right hon. friend ought to tell us here and now what are the contents of the ref-

erence which has been made to Judge Davidson. I pause for a reply.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: A copy of the Order in Council is here; it will be laid on the table of the House to-night. I handed it just now to the Minister of Justice; I will send it over to my hon. friend.

At this juncture I
might as well' read this document. It is dated the 9th of May, and is as follows:
The committee of the Privy Council have had before them a report dated 8th May, 1916, from the Minister of Justice submitting with reference to tne commission of 2nd June, 1915, issued to the Honourable Sir Charles Peers Davidson to investigate the purchase of arms and munitions, etc., and the expenditures and payments therefor, that it is deemed desirable to extend the powers of the commissioner so as to enable him to inquire into and investigate the facts and circumstances of or connected with the sale or disposal by Your Royal High, ness's Government of small arm munitions since 4th August, 1914, referred to in returns made to the House of Commons on the 1st and 2nd of May, 1916.
The minister therefore recommends that Your Royal Highness cause inquiry to be made pursuant to part 1 of the Inquiries Act, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906, chapter 104, concerning the aforesaid transactions and that a supplementary commission be issued in the case conferring and charging upon the commissioner all the powers and duties for the inquiry aforesaid which the commissioner has under and by virtue of the aforesaid commission of 2nd June, 1915.
The committee concur in the foregoing recommendation and submit the same for approval.
The Minister of Justice had the temerity to denounce my hon. friend for North Cape Breton for bringing on this resolution this afternoon because the Government had referred this matter to a commission. Yet no one ever saw this Order in Council outside of himself and the Prime Minister until this moment. The Minister of Justice really had the temerity to charge my hon. friend with having brought this question on for the purpose of discussing this matter in advance. That suggestion is not worthy of my hon. friend, and he would not have made it had he not been in a temper, and were it not for the fact that he was indulging in a species of buncombe such as I never heard him attempt to perpetrate in this House before.
The minister appealed to the House and the .country to regard with indignation the suggestion made toy my right hon. leader that Captain John 'Thompson, wearing as he does the King's uniform, engaged as he ought to be and no doubt is, in preparing himself to go overseas, and being a subordinate for the time
being of the Minister of Militia and, as the Minister of Justice knows, under his control and direction, would .place himself in an anomalous position by continuing to act in that investigation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Hear, hear.

As a friend of Captain John Thompson, as a professional man, I want to say that tooth from a military and a legal -standpoint, and in view of all the ethics that apply to the professions both of law and of arms, my friend Captain John Thompson knows that he would occupy a most anomalous .position before the -people of this country if he undertook to go on with an investigation into the conduct of the man -who is, at this -moment, his superior of&cer. Such a suggestion as was made toy my right hon. friend was an eminently proper one. My hon. friend's criticism was pure buncombe and .playing to the gallery, and my hon. friend knows it very well. Not only was it unworthy of him, but I venture to say that I never saw him .before descend to such tactics in discussing a public question. He complains because this resolution was introduced. Why sir, what are the facts of the case? The story is a long one. On March 9, over two -months ago, I ventured to ask this question in the House:
Mr. Macdonald:
1.	Was any small arms ammunition disposed of by the Militia Department since August 4, 1914? If so, to whom?
2.	What was the price received?
Mr. Kemp:	All serviceable ammunition has
been issued to Canadian contingents. It would not be advisable to give the details during the present emergency, in the public Interest.
The moment I saw that answer in Hansard I knew, as every hon. gentleman who read it must have known, that there was something very peculiar in regard to the question of the sale of small arms ammunition. I had no detailed information in regard to the matter; I had no means of knowing whether there was anything incorrect in the transaction. But -the very answer given by the Minister of Militia at that time was an indication that he was concealing something that 'was suspicious. I proceeded to put further questions, and, quite unconscious of the fact that the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carviell) * was moving along the same lines, and without any communication with him, I asked, on March 14, a general * question in regard to the whole matter, while my hon. friend

asked a similar question on March 13. These questions remained unanswered for quite a number of days. On March 23rd my question was put and this occurred:
Mr. Macdonald:
1.	Did any one purchase from the Militia Department, since August 4, 1914, any small arms ammunition?
2.	If so, what quantity, and what price was
paid therefor?	.
3.	Who was the purchaser?
Mr. Kemp : Stand.
Mr. Macdonald: How long does my hon. friend expect this question to stand. It has stood for two weeks now.
Mr. Kemp: We will give the information just as soon as possible. We are doing everything possible in that direction.
'One would think it wae necessary to make some very involved and deep exploration in order to answer the question; yet all the papers relating to the transactions were lying in the Militia Department, and the transactions 'bad been closed on the 1st day of January, 1916, and every hon. gentleman comprising the Government knew that a memorandum had come to council and had never been passed. Yet the Acting Minister of Militia wanted the House to believe that he was straining every energy to get this information in order to give it to the House. Finally, on March 27, an answer was given to the question of my hon. friend from Carleton. That answer was to the effect that this ammunition, which we are told to-day is no good at all, had been sold lor money to various rifle clubs throughout the Dominion for the use of men who were practising and learning to shoot. ' At the end of the answer there came this statement:
To Vickers, Limited, a certain number of rounds of Mark VI, at $20 per thousand rounds represented to be for the purpose of testing machine guns.
The sale of a quantity of ammunition to Vickers-Maxim to be used for testing machine guns, coupled with the suspicious circumstances in connection with the returns up to that time, at once suggested to one's mind that here was a field in which further information might be desired. So following that, on March 29, I moved for an Order of the House, and I was met by my right hon. friend (Sir Robert Borden), who told me that it was contrary to the public interest to disclose the quantity of ammunition that was sold. My right hon. friend indicated that I must amend my motion before I could have it passed. I was compelled to amend the motion, eliminating the matter of quantity, because, for-TMr. Macdonald.j
sooth, there was liable to a national menace if the quantity were published. All this time the quantity that was sold, apart from the sale to Vickers-Maxim, was sold to people in this country foT practising with the rifle, rifle clubs and organizations of that kind, so that the theory that the disclosure of the quantities would be liable to hurt somebody or be dangerous to the public interest was entirely illusory; it had'no justification whatever.
What follows? On April 6 my question was answered. Varying slightly in terms from that of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell), it had been dropped from the Order Paper in my absence from the House on the theory that the answer to the question of the hon. member for Carleton was a sufficient answer to my question-tion. I was compelled to call the attention of the House to the fact that I had asked for certain information and that my question varied from that of the hon. member for Carleton. It was not until April 5 that my question was answered. On April 5, in a discussion with my hon. friend on the subject, he said:
I have no objection to this motion passing, subject, of course, to some consideration as to giving the quantities. I shall also endeavour to expedite it.
From April 5 to May 1 nothing was done with regard to bringing down the return, but on May 1, two months after we had started to get the most ordinary information in regard to this matter, the return was formally brought down. These facts indicate a condition of affairs which naturally would cause suspicion to be aroused in the public mind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
On what date
was the order passed by the House?
April 5.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
When was the
return brought down?
On May 1.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is not two months.

Two months, I said, elapsed from the time at which the matter was first broached in the House until the Government were able to bring down the return. My right hon. friend was not then in charge of the department, but the acting minister who was in charge knew that the subject was not only a matter of interest but that it was to come up in the

House and he ought to have been able to have got the return in much less time than it took. Well, the return was brought down. It goes into a lot of ancient documents that have no relevancy whatever to the question. Notwithstanding this unnecessary and irrelevant matter, what does the return disclose, beyond the shadow of a doubt? It discloses this and I speak from the official statement:
On September 8. 1915, Col. J. W. Allison, representing the Vickers, Limited, applied to purchase 236,000 rounds of Mark VI ammunition required by Sir Trevor Dawson.
Application approved by the minister.
These hon. gentlemen talk about the *Quartermaster General having the sale of bad ammunition. Any theory of that kind, such as we heard put before the House this afternoon, vanishes in the face of the official statement. I find on page 13 of the return:
Application approved by the minister. The shipment in question was made on September 22.
On December 18 Col. Allison applied for 2,000000 rounds of Mark VI ammunition.
Application approved by the minister.
No Quartermaster General is selling that ammunition. The minister sells it as this document shows. Imagine the temerity of hon. gentlemen in talking about bad ammunition and the Quartermaster General having power to sell it. It seems absurd in the face of this positive statement that this application was approved by the minister. Then:
On November 11, Col. Allison applied for
1.000.	000 rounds of Mark VI ammunition for his principals.
Application approved by minister.
Later Col. Allison asked that this amount be increased to 2,000,000.' This was authorized to be issued-
By the minister.
On December 18, Col. Allison applied for
2.000.	000 rounds of Mark VI ammunition.
He applied in a telegram from New York in which he said he was there with the minister and that the minister had authorized the sale of this ammunition, but he wanted to let the Quartermaster General know about it. Inquiry was made by the proper officials to know if this quantity should be issued and at what price and it was:
Approved by minister-
On the 20th December, 1915.
-later endorsed by minister to ascertain by whom to be used, and if sold, to be by Order in Council. The deputy minister endorsed the
application that this sale would only be by Order in Council.
Then we have the
Application for Order in Council as Anally settled.
There was a memorandum from the minister asking the Governor General in Council for approval not merely for the sale of the balance of the 5,000,000 rounds of ammunition but for approval of the sale that he had effected without any Order in Council permitting him to do so. There the matter stood. No Order in Council was ever passed, and as my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition pointed out this afternoon, the result was that a Minister of the Crown undertook to sell the property of the Canadian people without the authority or consent of the Crown which, under the law, he must and should have got before undertaking to dispose of that property.
These are the facts in connection with the matter. When you remember that this gentleman, Mr. J. Wesley Allison, was the man who negotiated this unusual and peculiar sale, you have a further condition under which investigation' becomes absolutely imperative. Mr. J. Wesley Allison went to the minister first in regard to the purchase of this ammunition and the minister sent him to the Quartermaster General. Mr. J. Wesley Allison writes the Quartermaster General telling him, and his letter is to be found at page 16 of the return:
Referring to my arrangements with you some time ago for the purchase of 236,000,-303 Mark VI cartridges for Sir Trevor Dawson, I have just received a cable requesting me to have these shipped.
J. Wesley Allison arranges with the Minister of Militia that he is to get this quantity and then he writes to the Quartermaster General for the purpose of getting it. He writes to the Quartermaster General that he has been instructed by the minister to apply to him for the purpose of getting the ammunition. Then we find a statement made to the House and made in the memorandum accompanying the application for the Order in Council to the effect that this ammunition was required for testing purposes. There is not a line or word in any of these documents on record to show that the Vickers Maxim Company ever asked to get this ammunition for testing purposes. That is purely the creation of the minister in preparing the memorandum for council. No one of his subordinates made a statement of that kind. It is not here stated from any source that it was to be used for

testing purposes. Yet, the Government undertake to ratify that assertion by stating to Parliament, in answer to my hon. friend from Carleton, that they had sold a large quantity of this ammunition to the Vickers Company to be used for testing purposes. I would like to know where the minister who answered that question got that information. Is it to be found in any document? If it is contained in any document it should have been brought down. This House was entitled to see that document and to know whether the Vickers Maxim Company wanted this ammunition for testing purposes. It turns out when the minister does bring down the return, that he has placed on file a memorandum, a sort of apology or excuse or justification for the sale in which he intimates that this ammunition was not used for testing purposes at all but that it was wanted by the British Government.
Right here I want to ask the right hon. gentleman who leads the House what possible explanation he has for a department of this Government selling ammunition or anything else to the British Admiralty through the intervention of Col. J. W. Allison. If the British Admiralty wanted to buy ammunition, how is it that my right hon. friend was not communicated with? How is it that the British Admiralty did not communicate their wishes to this Government in the proper and official way? But that is not the situation; J. W. Allison appears in this transaction. This House and country is being absolutely deceived by the official statement made to the House that this ammunition was sold to Vickers-Maxim for testing purposes. It was not sold to Vickers-Maxim for testing purposes; the Government knows that, and the	Minister of Militia
knows . it.	But in some way this
ubiquitous individual, J. W. Allison, who turns up at every corner in this country where there is a dollar to be made, is thrust into the position of mid-10 p.m. dleman between this Government and the British Admiralty. My right hon. friend took very great care this afternoon not to refer to J. W. Allison. He said nothing whatever to defend or excuse him, or even irfdicate that he had any existence at all. True, the Minister of Militia once more rushed to the defence of his friend in his usual vigorous style; but the right hon. -gentleman left J. W. Allison alone; he was not going to father him. He has not assumed Macdonald.]
any responsibility for him up to date, although this afternoon he did endeavour to assume responsibility for the righteousness of the sale of this ammunition. But he was not going to assume responsibility for J. W. Allison. He told us that this ammunition was no good. Why was it no good? Because it was under suspicion. And he quoted Colonel Barlow's report that the ammunition was not to be used in Mark II rifles.
And yet the ammunition was sold. During the past year I find that Major J. S. Thom, of Sarnia, for instance, purchased 1,000 rounds of this very same ammunition; the Prince Edward Island Provincial Rifle Association also purchased a large quantity; the Amherst Canadian Rifle Association purchased 1,000 rounds of this ammunition on two occasions; the 63rd Regiment, in the constituency of my hon. friend, purchased 4,754 rounds of this very same ammunition, which the minister says he will never allow to get into the hands of our boys who are fighting at the front. But he is willing to let the 63rd Regiment take the chance of shooting themselves while practising rifle shooting with this ammunition; he did not care about them. Then the 183rd Rifle Association purchased 1,100 rounds; the Mor-ven Canadian Rifle Association, 600 rounds, and the 20th " B " Horse.

What did they pay?
iMr. MACDONALD: The price varied according to the amount purchased. Some paid $20, and here it says that $25 was paid by the 20th " B " Horse, but it does not indicate whether that was the price per thousand rounds, or for the total quantity bought.
What did the Minister of Militia mean this afternoon when he talked about the Quartermaster General having power to dispose of this ammunition without an Order in Council? Did he want the House to believe that Quartermaster General Macdonald had sold this ammunition without his authority? If he did not mean that, what was he talking about the Quartermaster General for? In addition to the names given in the main return, there appears in the supplementary return a list of other parties to whom this ammunition was sold. Under the authority of the Minister of Militia we find that Vickers, Limited, of London, bought 236,000, 2,000,000 and 750,000 rounds at different times. The man who was responsible and whose authority was given for the sale of

these three lots is given in the official document as the hon. Minister of Militia. It is clearly proven beyond the shadow of a doubt in regard to these various items that the Minister of Militia himself directed the sale of the ammunition to Allison. There is nothing in these returns to indicate for one minute that the ammunition was to be used for testing purposes. The first time any suggestion .was made about its .being used for testing purposes was in the memorandum sent by the minister to Council on the 5th of January.
It appears further from this return, from the statement of the minister himself justifying this transaction, that the sale was not to Vickers-Maxim at all, but that the ammunition ultimately went to the British Admiralty. These are the facts, unquestioned and undoubted, that are given in the return. These are the facts that the Government was fooling with from March 5 to May 1, and were preventing from getting >to the public. I should like to ask the Prime Minister why the answer was given on March 5 that serviceable ammunition . had been issued to all Canadian contingents, but that in the public interest it would not be advisable to give details during the present emergency. Why was that answer given if it was not to prevent the information from being given to the public? The defence made this afternoon was that the Quartermaster General had disposed of this ammunition, but I have proved from the return that he did not sell it, and that it was sold1 directly under the authority of the minister. Other documents in the return indicate that in December the minister and Allison were conferring in New York, and wired up to Ottawa that a large quantity of ammunition be provided, but the deputy minister made a memorandum, which is on the return here, to the effect that the requisition -would have to go to Council for sanction. So much for the Quartermaster General and his poweT.
My right hon. friend this afternoon went at great length into Colonel Barlow's report as to the quality of the ammunition. It is needless for the Minister of Militia to make assertions -that he is not going to let any of his boys at the front fight with this ammunition, as if there was any chance of them getting bad ammunition unless he put it into their hands. He need not make doughty assertions of that kind, as if we were forcing bad ammunition upon them. Who is doing that? No one. If this ammunition was of no value why did the
British Admiralty want it, and why did this Government sell it to them through its own minister? If the ammunition was no good, -why did they put through a transaction, through their own middlemen, whereby the boys on the ships -and in the naval brigades in England were provided with ammunition which the minister would not allow the boys in the Canadian regiments to use? Having regard to the fact that all the forces of the Empire are one, what difference does it make whether the ammunition explodes in the rifle in the hands of a boy in one of the naval brigades in England, or in the hands of a Canadian soldier? Why should an attempt be made to mislead the public in regard to this ammunition? Why is it asserted that the ammunition was of no value, when the British Admiralty got it and used it? And this Government knew that the British Admiralty got it and used it. If they knew this ammunition was no good, they were guilty of a crime against the state and against the Empire in permitting improper ammunition to go into the hands of any portion of the forces of the Empire. Yet they did that, and they kept on selling to the men in the rifle club throughout this country this ammunition for practice. It is no wonder that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister came to the conclusion that the matter deserved to be investigated. The question is as to whether he is going to give that full and complete investigation which he avowed to the country he was prepared to do in regard to all matters. He can choose two tribunals, both in existence at the present time, one presided over by two distinguished judges with ample counsel representing all possible parties, a tribunal in active operation which can proceed with the inquiry at once. My right hon. friend said that there were witnesses available in town which could be heard at once. Who were the witnesses? Col. J. Wesley Allison is in town. Does my right hon. friend mean to say that that gentleman may -skip out before the Meredith-Duff Commission would get through with him in regard to this matter? What other witnesses are in town? This transaction is not one in which Americans are involved; it is a transaction in which men of the British race are involved, and I am quite sure that if it is necessary to get information from England, means could be adopted to get that information. We are not dealing with aliens in this matter, and it is within the purview of the

Meredith-Duff Commission if my right hon. friend would give it the poweT to deal with the matter. His only excuse for not giving them that power is that there were some witnesses in town.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is not correct.
What is the excuse?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is not an excuse; it is a reason. The reason was that the Meredith-Duff Commission had been appointed to deal with expenditures made by the British Government. The Sir Charles Davidson 'Commission had oeen appointed to deal with matters that directly concerned this Government, as that matter does. Therefore, it was thought advisable that it should be referred to that commission.

If my right hon. friend will pardon me, that is not a very good reason, and if he will stop to think for a moment, he will see that this is peculiarly a matter that ought to go before the Meredith-Duff Commission, because it is a matter affecting the sale of ammunition by this Government to the British Government. According to the facts that are admitted, the British Government purchased from this Government certain small arms ammunition.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not admit anything of the kind. I have already stated that no such proposal ever came to the attention of the Government, so far as I am aware. The proposal that came to the Government was that this ammunition should be sold or its sale ratified to Vickers, Limited, of England.
This is the statement of the minister himself. My right hon. friend has seen this memorandum.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What does the hon. member say contrary to that?

The memorandum
says:
It is understood that, to cover the cost of transport, handling-, exchange, insurance, etc., a sum was added, hy one of Vickers' officers, to the price, but, on learning that these expenditures were borne by the British Government, they were immediately removed.
My hon. friend the Minister of Militia this afternoon stated that this ammunition went to the British Admiralty.
[Mr. Macdonald.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Does not the statement that my hon. friend holds in his hand state definitely that the ammunition was sold to Vickers, Limited?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That was what I was alluding to.
But it was resold by Vickers, Limited, to the Admiralty, according to the statement of the Minister of Militia this afternoon.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not remember that.

Not only that, but he says in this memorandum:
The assurance was given that not one cent was paid in commission hy the firm to any one, and no profit was made on it. It is understood that, to cover the cost of transport, handling, exchange, insurance, etc., a sum was added, by one of Vickers' officers, to the price, but, on learning that these expenses were borne by the British Government, they were immediately removed.
Those munitions went to the British Government; they went to the Admiralty. I say this is essentially a case that ought to have gone to the Meredith-Duff Commission because it referred to relations between this Government and the Admiralty in regard to ammunition. The Meredith-Duff Commission was the proper tribunal; the counsel were there, everything was in readiness to proceed; J. Wesley Allison was before the commission or going to be before it. My right hon. friend must admit that it was an unnecessary and unusual act on his part when he proceeded to resurrect Sir Charles Davidson. and hand the matter over to 'him. We have the question before the House and the country as to which would be the better tribunal, and after a long discussion this evening, the Minister of Justice indicated that he might be prepared to appoint counsel, but he was very careful in regard to that; he was making very large reservations in regard to what he was going to do, and he did not speak with frankness in regard to the subject. I say that the Davidson Commission is not the proper commission to try this matter. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister knows that; he knows that Sir Charles Davidson is a jurist who has retired from the bench; that he is a very old gentleman; that the task of dealing with this matter or any matter of an investigation is one that requires strenuous virility on the part of any judge. I remember, when my right hon. friend was leading the Opposition, that the present Mr. Justice Lennox,

who was one of his lieutenants, discussed year in and year out the lack of wisdom in appointing judges as commissioners to deal with matters of this kind. I say without hesitation that the Sir Charles Davidson Commission is not one which has the confidence of the country at the present time.
Just let us see what was said to-day in one of our papers in regard to the subject.
- I agree that in this country the maintenance of the fair name of the judiciary is one of the highest possible importance, because anything that would create a lack of confidence in the mind of the public in the men who have to sit as judges would be an unfortunate thing for the people and for the state. This is a letter which I think is worthy of the attention of the House:
The following is some of the evidence given by Mr. Allison as it appeared in the press report of the 8th instant, before the Davidson commission
Have you any letter to act as agent for General Hughes?-No, I had letters of introduction from him and I found the minister's influence was of great assistance to me.
Was the introduction to the Colt Company one?-I am not sure. X think I knew the Colt officers before that, but not in a business way.
" I am to understand," asked Sir Charles, " that while you had letters of introduction from General Hughes you never utilized them?" -Not for business, but for social purposes.
Is there anything in that evidence which would possibly give Sir Charles Davidson to understand ' that while you had letters of introduction from General Hughes you never utilized them'? Is this not rather the evidence of Commissioner Davidson than of Allison? Then look at Allison's answer.
So says the wily Allison.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Who signs the
letter?
The letter is anonymous.
Oh, oh.

The fact that it is an anonymous letter does not make any difference because it draws an inference which an eminent lawyer like my right hon. friend would draw himself. The letter goes on:
-and yet Allison says at the commencement that he found "the minister's influence was of great assistance to him." Socially or commercially, which did he mean? We don't know who he met socially; we know what he did commercially. Is it any wonder the public grin when they read the report of a commission such as this?-Reader.
My hon. friend the Minister of Justice dilated upon the tremendous work of this commission and the fact that it had been sitting for a year.
Anyone who stops to think will realize that what Judge Davidson has been doing is trying a number of different cases during the past year, just as every judge who sits in the Supreme Court of any of our provinces. But, although he has been trying these cases, and began to deal with them last autumn-September or even earlier- he has never given judgment in a single one. What is the reason he does not decide in regard to the question of the purchase of horses in Kings County," Nova Scotia? He tried that case last fall. It has no relation to anything that he is trying today. Any judge would be almost driven off the Bench, or, at the very least, difficulty would be raised, if he should reserve judgment as long as Sir Charles Davidson has reserved judgment in this case. Everybody knows that Mr. Foster, the gentleman who was concerned in that matter, is telling his friends that he is going to be whitewashed, and that he will be the candidate of the party in Kings County again. My right hon. friend (Sir Robert Borden) has heard that.
Sir ROBERT BORDEN I have heard nothing of the kind.

Then all I can say
is that the right hon. gentleman is getting very badly out of touch with his own home constituency. Is there any warrant under heaven for Sir Charles Davidson, who tried that case in. regard to the Kings County horses not giving judgment? That is what the people of the county are asking. It is a very singular thing that even though the evidence in these cases is all in, this gentleman cannot take time to consider the question of fact involved and sit down and write a judgment. Though Parliament has been sitting for four months, and though we have asked that some suggestion be made that this report should be brought down, we are going to close next week and there will be no report. And there may be no report when we come together for next session. Yet the Prime minister in giving another case to this judge who never decides anything, another case to be put away, never to be decided and never heard tell of. Had my hon. friend committed the task of inquiry in this matter to the Meredith-Duff Commission, he knows there would be a finding within a reasonable time. If it is given to Sir Charles Davidson, who has worked so hard that he cannot decide the cases he tried nearly a year ago, when can we hope for a declaration from the commissioner as to his opinion on the facts of the case?
