speechtext: Motion agreed to, and the House went into Committee of Supply.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Rhodee in the Chair.
Canadian Northern Railway Company-loan not exceeding $15,000,000.

Mr. Chairman, I desire to make a few observations in order to have them placed on Hansard and to direct them to the attention of the Government, particularly of the Minister of Finance, and the Minister of the Interior. I purpose making them upon this item. The problem of the best solution of our railway question is one that I cannot discuss in any very full way. Different speakers have had different solutions to offer, and different observations to make. The observation that I desire to make is that there is one way to render our railways successful, and that is to develop our country, especially the West, in such a way that there will be more business for the railways. The facts and figures which I propose to offer on that bear out



the contention I desire to make, namely that we have at our disposal in Western Canada an enormous quantity of arable land which, if put to use as it was meant to be, would give a sufficient production of wealth in this country to enable us to better bear our burdens, speaking in a general sense, and would afford increased business for the railways. The three railways we have on our hands, I suppose, like other business concerns, are for the purpose of doing business. No business man, and no association of business men, having established a great factory or plant, would say that they had arrived at the goal which was before them when they had merely constructed their plant. The building of our railways is in itself only a means towards an end. It is worse than useless to build railways unless you are going to use them. It is worse than useless to build a factory unless you are going to use your brains to get grist for your mi'll, goods to manufacture, and markets in which to sell them. We in Canada have these railways, and they have a certain thing to sell, namely transportation; and you cannot sell transportation unless there is something to transport and unless there are men who are able to pay for that transportation, or, in other words, are able to buy the thing that you are ready to offer on the market. While there may be many suggestions to be made as to other ways in which this principle might be applied, such as in the development of our manufacturing industries, I, coming from the West, wish to call the attention of the committee to something which I think worthy of the attention of this House and of this country, from the viewpoint of the great resources we have lying in the West.
Last year we had in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, and I speak of those two provinces alone, nearly 15,000,000 of acres of land under cultivation. I take the figures from the statistical departments of this Government. The total amount of arable land which is at our disposal in those two western provinces is 190,000,000. We had 15,000,000 acres, approximately, under cultivation, producing wealth for this nation, and 175,000,000 acres lying idle. There must be some reason for this. There must be something that is standing in the way of ' using that great national resource that we have there, and my point this evening is, without any reference to party issues whatever, that whatever is standing in the way of the development of these western acres, surely there must be in Canada brains

enough to find out how to use and develop and make productive that great national asset that is lying there, not being developed in any way. Of course we cannot develop it all in a day, or in a year, or perhaps in a decade. During recent years, and I shall not weary the House with comparative figures, we have not been stretching out our arms to take into the national use these great national assets. We are not developing in the direction of even gradually exploiting that great national asset which lies before us. Last year according to the statistics of the Government, and I have no reason to doubt their accuracy, the value of the crops produced on those 15,000,000 acres in those two western prairie provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, was over three hundred million dollars. If we could apply the same proportion to these unused arable lands, we would have, not three hundred million dollars, but three billion, nine hundred million dollars. When we are through with this war we are going to have an enormous debt; it may be one billion dollars; it may be two billio l dollars. The interest on it will be probably fifty million dollars per annum at the least. Here there lies in our hands and in our possession 175,000,000 acres of land which, if they were to produce at the rate the acres in use last year yielded, would produce in one year three billion, nine hundred million dollars worth of produce, a value four times as great as this terrible war debt that is staring us in the face. I desire to say to this Government, and especially to my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior, that the responsibility that rests upon him at this time is very great. We have other resources. We have the fisheries, the mines, the lumber; we have our industries, our manufacturing plants, and all of these can, no doubt co-operate, and can in a very great way help us to meet this tremendous obligation that is before us. But, all said and done, while I may be partial to the West, and, like many a western man, may think more of it in a comparative sense than I ought to think, yet. when you see lying there, unused, 175,000,000 acres of land, you must realize that we have in our hands an asset that it is our duty to develop to the greatest degree possible.
There may be some difficulties in bringing this about. Of course there is the difficulty of immigration, and of that I shall say nothing, because there are reasons why to-day, and for the last two or three years, we are not able to achieve a'l we should like. But I make this suggestion to the

Minister of the Interior and to the Minister of Finance, that, in the case of such of this land which is lying idle as is owned by private owners, they should penalize the holding of that land in such a way that men would have to use it. Men are holding enormous stretches of land, within 5, 10 or 20 miles of the railways, . just waiting for the rise of the market. They went in at the low prices, they went in for the purpose of speculating and trafficking in the unearned increment of this country ; and I declare that I would penalize the holding of this land. That may seem a strong word, and there are many upon whom it would bear very hardly; but the financial desperateness of our country is going to be such that I would feel quite justified', for my part, in penalizing men who hold land not for use, because we have no time in Canada to-day to waste pity on the men who want to lie still and wait for the unearned increment to make millionaires of them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would that not be a matter for the Provincial Governments rather than for the Dominion?
I think the observation of the Minister of Finance is well taken, and I had that in mind when I said that surely there are in Canada men who could devise some remedy.
Are not the provinces in the West doing that now by the super-tax?

They are doing it now in a degree, about $10 per quarter-section. But that is not meeting the purpose that I have in view. It is true that this matter really comes under the provincial jurisdiction, but we are a democracy, and surely no man will say that because it happens, by the accident of our constitution, that the provinces have a more direct and more customary control of the taxation of land, we are going to lie down and say that we can do nothing. Immigration is under the Federal jurisdiction; the administration of the war is under this Government; and those things to a certain extent would justify this Government in saying that the interest of trade and commerce, the interest of the war, the interest of immigration, require that this Parliament should exert its powers and pass such legislation as is necessary to ensure the cultivation of that land.
If it were only a matter of amending our constitution that would be in itself a very simple thing, These provinces down here
248J
do not realize the necessity because the matter has not pressed itself upon them as it has upon us. This fetish of the British North America Act which you invoke when any change is proposed is only a fetish after all and it is a small thing to stand in the way of bringing under cultivation 175,000,000 acres of land. I think my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) would agree with me that in a democratic country like ours, possessing great resources, a great part of which belonged to the -prown, when you find great areas in the hands of speculators, men who are not using the land for cultivation, the question of amending the British North America Act is a very small thing to stand in the way of the cultivation of this land. Make it gradual. Undoubtedly it would force down the price of land.
Would my hon. friend give us an idea of what portion of the 175,000,000 acres is owned by the Crown and what portion is granted?

I am sorry 1 cannot do that. I might have anticipated that question and I recognize my oversight m not having informed myself on that point. But in regard to that which is owned by speculators, and there is an enormous quantity owned by private individuals, I would adopt means such as I have suggested. In regard to the other, surely we can get experts to advise us if the minister thinks the task is too large to be undertaken by himself. We have a countless number of commissioners trying to find out academic things, and you might as well try to find out what the moon is made out of for any good that that is going to do. If there ever was a commission that would be justified, I think it would be a commission that would tell us how to go about this question so as to enable men to get on these other lands which are still in the hands of the Crown. We aTe going to have 175,000 or 200,000 soldiers coming back from the war. Many of them will be able to work on the land while others will not. With all the modem agricultural machinery now in use, a man with an arm off, or otherwise incapacitated, can often do a great deal more work on the farm than he can in the city. I do not see any reason why a tax should not be put on companies, and on those men who are rich enough to hold land for speculation, and why you should not use that money for the purpose of developing the lands still in the hands of the Government. Surely something of that kind could be worked out in order that men could go on the land.
Is there not a scheme before one of the legislatures to put a tax of 30 cents an acre on uncultivated land? I understood there was such a proposal.

Yes, there is an extra charge of $10 on 160 acres of uncultivated land.
iMr. WRIGHT: But I understood there was a proposal to impose a tax of 30 cents an acre.

I am not aware of it. I was speaking only of my own province, and there, I understand, it is $10 per quarter section. The expense incurred in getting this thing under way would not be very great. It might have to start in a small way, but we should not allow that land to lie idle for such a long time. We cannot speak of conditions as if they were normal conditions. We can only speak of the last conditions we know of as being normal. In Moosejaw we had men walking the streets by scores who were crying out for work, men who wanted simply to make a living, and they could not get work of any kind. Out on the prairies there was this immense number of acres crying for men to come and work. There was something wrong when these two could not be brought together-the men seeking work and the land 'belonging to this Government crying out for men to come and work it. Then we saw that there was no encouragement for these two to 'be brought together. The raw material was there, and the men were there ready to exercise their muscle on the raw material, but the conditions were not sufficiently encouraging to bring the two together. Surely we could make these conditions encouraging enough to bring these two elements together. You are bonusing every kind of industry. By protection you are bonusing them all. It may be hard to work out, but surely we can work out some system by which men will go on the land and use it for the purpose for which it was meant to be used. No doubt the minister can throw many difficulties in the way. Suppose a man owned one section of land instead of the millions of acres we own. He has been a man of comparative wealth before and has had no trouble in meeting his payments. But, suppose he met with reverses and had to live more economically, to use other resources for his income, the first thing he would do would	be to go to his
section of land and .start work at 
farming. I have seen many a man in Moosejaw do the same thing. A man got "busted" in real estate, ot in trading jack knives that had been making a fortune for him, he took his land and he is doing better than he ever did before. We, the Government, are in one sense a great big farmer with an immense farm of 175,000,000 acres, we are in a desperate position financially and we have the ability to produce $3,900,000,000 worth of grain in one year. Why not use that immense farm in such a manner as to increase our income and thus create a business that will make us able to meet our financial obligations?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. J. EOCHE (Minister of the Interior) :
speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Just a few words in regard to western land settlement. I quite agree that we have a very large area of unsettled land but it must be remembered that a very large proportion has already 'been alienated from the Crown. It has passed into the hands of railway companies in the form of land grants. Whether we have had a judicious system in the past or not it would be altogether useless to discuss at the present time. In the early history of Canada it was absolutely essential to 'hold out extraordinary inducements to get the great West opened up by means of railways and as a consequence of this a very large acreage was alienated from the Crown. There is also a large area in the hands of private speculators, land companies and individuals, in addition to regular homesteaders and others holding Government land. The question of compelling these people to bring this land undeT cultivation is a very important one, a very complex one and one which more directly comes within provincial jurisdiction. The provincial legislatures have attempted to grapple with it during the last few years by means of taxing wild land and a surtax on uncultivated land. I do not know of anything that they have quoted in the United States to discredit immigration very much more, with the exception of conscription, than the question of provincial taxation.
Or the duty on grain.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
No, I heard very little about the duty on grain when I was there. A great deal of fault has been fotmd on the part of residents of the United States with the provincial taxation on land companies. Eepresentatives of these companies have been down here giving their

evidence before the Economic Development Commission, complaining bitterly of the discouragement to the investment of capital in Canada by reason of the very large taxation that has been put on land by means of that surtax. I am not finding any fault with the local legislatures for having adopted that policy. I think it is the best policy to penalize people who are holding out uncultivated land in order that it may be brought under cultivation. But at the same time it has its side of criticism and the premier of Saskatchewan, when I invited him to attend the conference of immigration agents in February, , devoted almost his entire remarks to a justification of his Government in imposing this surtax.
One thing the American papers have made a great deal of in trying to keep die American farmers at home has been the printing of facsimiles of the tax notices sent out through western Canada. In one column they will show general taxes, in another school taxes, and in another gopher taxes, and so on, giving the American people the impression that the Canadians are taxed to death. America is, of course, more thickly populated and their lands are higher priced than ours, and the American farmers would not look so much to the total of these taxes as to the number of different items, and those interested in discouraging immigration have made the utmost possible capital out of this. The hon. gentleman has said that this is a large question which should be referred to some commission. That has been done already. The Economic Commission has been working on it during the past year.
Were the commissioners selected for their fitness to grapple with an economic question of this kind?

It is an honorary commission, but an honorary commi sion is, as a rule, composed of competent and representative men. This commission is comprised of farmers, business men, land men, transportation men-representative men from every province of the Dominion almost. I think it is a very good commission.
It is too big.

They can collect information just the same as any other* commission; I know that they have had this question under consideration, and that they have had a number of witnesses before them. Perhaps they are not getting on as expeditiously as we should like, but Senator
Lougheed, of course, has been very busy during the session and probably has not had the time that he would otherwise have been able to devote to it. In this problem of land 'settlement the provincial Governments should act in co-operation with the Dominion. The provincial Governments themselves have a great deal to do with land settlement. I think one of the essential questions for Canada to determine is what we are going to do with the immigrants who come to this country after the war. I am afraid we are going to have-a large immigration, probably of those who-have never been brought up on the farm, and who know little about agriculture. To-put these men on the farm without previous agricultural experience and without: capital would be useless. They must have-training of some kind, either at an agricultural college or by seeing the demonstrations or experimental Farms, and so on. That is a matter that should be taken jp by the provincial Governments. Manitoba is grappling with it already. They set aside a sum of money last session to purchase stock to assist poor farmers. These men, of course, have to be hand-picked. Then there is the system of agricultural credits. A few years ago I understand that the various Governments in the West sent a commission to nearly every country in Europe and the United States, gathering evidence on this question. The commissioners made a report to their respective Governments as to the policy that should be pursued with regard to agricultural credits, but T do not think there has been any practicat outcome as yet. In Saskatchewan some law was placed on the statute-book, but it has not been taken advantage of. I think we should do everything we can to encourage those who come out to this country to go upon the land. That would involve the expenditure of a very large sum of money; there is no question about that; and that is one reason why, at the present time, when all our energies should be devoted to the winning of the war, we should not launch out upon any expenditure in this direction. As a matter of fact I do not look for any large immigation to Canada until after the war is over. History teaches us that there is little immigration to any country at war. But after the war I think we shall have abundance of immigration although I will not pledge myself that it will be of the kind that we have been endeavouring to secure-that is, agriculturists. We have had a very large immigration in years gone by. In the year ending

March 31, 1914, 385,000 immigrants came to Canada, and in the year before, 402,000- the largest number in the history of Canada. It may be true that not so many are taking up homesteads, but that is not a good criterion by which to judge. Many of these immigrants did not go to our western provinces at all, but located in the East. Then many of those who went out to the West went out as agricultural labourers, and never put in homestead entries. For the years ending March 31, 1914, and March 31, 1915, there was a larger immigration into the province of Ontario than into the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta combined. So you cannot say that the immigration is not of the Tight sort, simply judging by the homestead entries. I quite realize the importance of the subject the hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) has brought before the House. We expect a report from the Economic Commission in the very near future. It does not necessarily follow that their recommendations will be adopted in toto, or even in part, but at any rate we shall have the benefit of what information they collect, and shall then be in a better position to judge what policy to adopt.

I think the question raised by the hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) is one of the most important this House could discuss. No one doubts that when this war is over Canada will have a tremendously large debt, with a large fixed sum to pay annually on account of interest and sinking fund. Unquestionably, also, if we can increase the population of Canada we shall lessen to just that extent the per capita payments on *that debt. For instance, if within the next ten years the population of Canada doubles our per capita payment will be halved. It is quite true, as the minister says, that a great part of the 175,000,000 acres that the hon. member for Moosejaw spoke of has passed into the hands of private owners, and there is ho object in going into that subject now. But there is in the northern part of the three Prairie Provinces many millions of acres that are not prairie lands in the sense that the plains of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta are. In that area north of the Saskatchewan river from lake Winnipeg westerly there is a large stretch of park lands north of Prince Albert. There are some stretches of prairie and great stretches of timber land; but the timber is mostly poplar, and poplar is nearly always found on dry land. It is first class land when it is cleared up,

and grow splendid crops. Every one in the West knows that poplar bush is easy to clear up; the stumps come out very easily, or in the course of a few years they will rot out. When you get as far west as Edmonton, that class of country extends four or five hundred miles north of the Saskatchewan river, and in some places a great deal more, and as you go further west, the country is much more open. Probably only pant of that country could be called first class land, as compared with the country in the southern portions of the province, but it is very well suited for mixed farming. I know that in the southern portion of the province of Saskatchewan there are districts that are not well suited for raising wheat; where, although a good deal of wheat is grown, at the same time the land is more suited for mixed farming. My hon. friend will know, because it is the country he lives in, that there are some parts a little north and west of that that are better for stock raising than wheat. The farmers who, during the last 25 years, have gone into those parts that I have mentioned and have gone in for mixed farming, are the farmers who are most prosperous to-day. In my own constituency, on the eastern and northern side of the Moose mountain, where the land is more broken up and rougher than the general run of the land, the farmers who have adopted the system of cattle-raising and mixed farming are to-day amongst the most prosperous settlers in the whole province of Saskatchewan. In that country to the north of the Saskatchewan river there are millions and tens of millions which some time in the future will be settled by a thrifty, contented and prosperous population that will pay its share of the revenues of the country. If you wish, however, to have that country bring forth its best resources, it will be advisable to give a certain amount of assistance to the settlers, and I have in mind a scheme somewhat along the following lines. Supposing a settler goes into that northern country and takes up one of those more or less rough quarter sections and builds a little house and stable, thus showing the Government that he is a bona fide settler, and that he knows how to handle his farm and to take care of cattle, I think, instead of doing as we have been doing for the last twenty years, spending a huge amount of money annually on public buildings and other public works throughout the country, many of them necessary and proper if times are prosperous, but unnece.-

sary in times such as we are having mw and such as we are going to have on account of the war and the railroad situation that is confronting us, the Government should commence a grant of, say, $1,000,000 a year, gradually increasing that amount to $5,000,000 or $10,000,000 a year, and appoint a body of men to buy cattle and give such settlers as I have described from two to ten cattle each according to his capacity for looking after them. Then they should charge that settler the full cost of the cattle laid down at his station, but charge him no interest on the cattle for, say, three years, then for a couple of years charge him interest on the cost, and then after he has had the cattle for five years, charge him a certain percentage of the cost so that at the end of ten years he will have paid back to the Government the cost of the cattle with five or six per cent interest according to the rate at which the Government could borrow the money. In that way you would have thousands and tens of thousands of settlers in that part of the country who would be making a living out of those cattle and who at the end of those ten years would be able to pay back the amount that was put into the cattle by selling off the increase as they grew up to be three or four years old. In that way, at the end of those ten years, those cattle would be paid back and the farmer would have a big herd of his own from the increase of the original stock. Even those who have watched what some farmers in our own neighbourhood, starting with a couple of cows, have done, can hardly appreciate how a herd increases and how a farmer can get a good herd around him. To make that scheme a success, care, of course, would have to be taken that stock would not be given to men who could not take care of them. That is one difficulty in the way, but difficulties are made to be overcome. Many of our settlers from the old country are men who come from the cities and do not understand the care of cattle, and it would be impossible for those men, in the course of one or two years, to know enough about the care of cattle to enable them to handle a proposition of that kind successfully. The average foreigner knows more about stock raising and can make money out of caring for cattle, so tbat the difficulty might arise that our English-speaking friend might say: You are not treating me as liberally as that foreigner. But the matter would have to be dealt with according to the merits and the ability of the man. If we would
take the money that we spend annually in unnecessary and unproductive work and put it into cattle, and distribute them amongst the settlers in that new country to the north, we would accomplish with that money ten times as much good as we could accomplish by spending it in the way that we have been doing in the past. Nineteen out oi twenty of those settlers would make a success, and the loss to the Government would be very little, if any. You would have to keep up that grant for, say, five years, and then, as the money came in from paying for stock, it could be put out again. I am merely outlining the scheme as I have it in mind, and when this Economic Commission reports, the matter can be taken up.
Would it be confined to the holders of unpatented lands?

My idea would be that in that country the land would be all unpatented for a number of years after the settlers went in. The Government could not only take security oh the stock itself, but could register a lien against the unpatented homestead. In case the land was patented, if there were any in that part of the country, to which the Government might apply under such an arrangement as this, security could be taken on the stock itself and also on the man's covenants, and, if the land was not encumbered, take security upon the land as well. I do not think there will be great difficulty in the matter of security. My hon. friend mentioned a few moments ago that something of that kind was being done in Manitoba. I discussed this matter with some of the members of the Government of Manitoba, and they told me they were going to make an experiment along that line applying to the country lying north of Winnipeg, which is very much the same class of country, as the minister is well aware, as that lying north of the Saskatchewan river in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. In fact, it was more wooded, I imagine, around Winnipeg. The difficulty they have had there is that of getting the land under cultivation for grain, but it is a good stock country, and any men in that part of the country who have been able to make a start in raising stock have done remarkably well. It will only take two or three years for the Government of Manitoba to try thi6 plan out and prove whether it is feasible or not. I remember that when I went into

that country first, about forty years ago- I settled in the vicinity of Manitou, Manitoba-certain people there who had a little money for investment would buy, say, ten head of cows and give them to a farmer on shares, the farmer to look after the stock and to give the capitalist or financial man one-half the increase when they ar* rived at three years of age. At the end of the term of agreement, five or ten years, the farmer had to return the ten head of cows. In the course of that time, the farmer would have a great big herd of cattle from half the increase, and the man who put up the money would have received a higher rate of interest than he could get iby loaning the money on mortgage) on farms, or in any other way. If the same success should attend the Government in furnishing the money, it would be a profitable thing for the settler and the Government would not lose anything. Even if action should not be taken for a year or two, the experience in Manitoba, I imagine, will have gone far enough to enable the Government to judge whether this scheme would appeal by them. No one would want to see such a thing tried on a very great scale at first, because it is, to an extent, experimental. The matter would have to be placed in the hands of somebody who would be absolutely outside of political control. I say that regardless of what Government is in office, or whether the Liberals or the Conservatives are in power. If this matter were the subject of political patronage that would go a long way to kill it, and would certainly make it unsuccessful. I feel sure that we have a huge stretch of country there that would be occupied by settlers, settlers who would become wealthy and will do just as well as they could in the best grain-growing parts of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, or Alberta. For many, many years to come cattle and stock of all kinds will command high prices. There will always be a market, and it does not matter in a case of that kind whether a man is forty or fifty miles away from a railroad. I lived for many years in the West, and I was in one case sixty miles and in another case further from the railway. Settlers who had cattle had no trouble in marketing, because, in a couple of days, they would drive out a big herd when it was ready for the market. I believe the suggestion I make to' the minister is worthy of consideration, for I have seen it carried out most successfully in individual cases. This plan will help to populate a 
country as large as the whole settled area of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta.
The Canadian Pacific are doing it now.

They are doing something along the same line, advancing money to settlers. But I have never been much in favour of putting men on lands in the West who had no money of their own, starting them out with a debt of $500 or $600 and expecting them to pay interest right along and pay the money back. But where a man has shown his ability as a farmer, and has the stabling, or can put it up, and will grow the hay in the vicinity, he will be all the better settler for having a little help and will not only pay back the money but, while he has it, his use of it will add materially to the wealth of the country and the revenues of the Government. It is getting near to Sunday morning, and I should think that the Government, whatever we may think on this side, will hardly feel like holding the House longer. I have an amendment of which I gave notice, and I would like to move it, as the chairman (Mr. Rhodes) has stated a point in regard to if. The resolution is as follows:
That after the word "approved" in the third line from the bottom of the particulars of the proposed vote, there should be added the following words: "Before making such loan the Governor in Council shall require the Company to give to His Majesty the King an option to acquire at any time within five years from the date thereof the railways and other property of the company and of all other railways and property included in the Canadian Northern system at such price as to the Governor in Council may seem reasonable under existing circumstances."
I do not propose to say anything in support of that amendment to-n,ight.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
We came here at two
o'clock expecting to get some business through. And here it is half-past eleven, and the hon gentleman proposes to adjourn with nothing done. Surely hon. gentlemen opposite have discussed this matter at sufficient length to have said everything that they desire to say concerning it. I think my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) has reduced everything that the other side desire to say into the motion he has presented, so I think hon. gentlemen opposite ought to be satisfied to vote on the motion and let us get the item through. My hon. friend knows that we are getting close to the end of the session. We are

hoping to prorogue on Tuesday and we have a considerable amount of business yet to do on Monday. If our hope of getting through on Tuesday is to be fulfilled, I would like my hon. friend to consider the idea of letting this item go through tonight if possible.

The minister can readily see that the reason why nothing was done to-day was because the Government would not let the proposed amendment carry. If it had carried, it could have been said that a great deal of progress had been made. We on this side of the House, therefore, are not to blame. The minister says very truly that in the discussion of the Grand Trunk Pacific item the Canadian Northern also was pretty fully discussed, but there are some gentlemen who want to express some views on the subject. Although I could give no definite assurance in the matter, I do not think the discussion would take very long, and I think I can assure the minister that every reasonable effort will be made to conclude the discussion in a comparatively short time. I do not think that much could be accomplished, at any rate, by remaining here for twenty-five more minutes to-night. So far as I am concerned, I will do the best I can to bring the discussion to a close on Monday at an early hour.

Just a word to the
Minister of the Interior. He intimated that I myself suggested the appointment of a commission. I wish to say distinctly that I feel it my duty to put the responsibility for that on the minister himself. If we are here next session I purpose bringing this matter up and making reference to the observation I have made this evening, 'est the minister might then say to me that I myself had suggested a commission. I say now that I suggested a commission only incidentally. It is the minister who has the responsibility. In these war days there is danger of ministers standing aside and watching the Minister of Militia and the Minister of Finance-particularly the Minister of Militia-look after itheir respective departments. I do not purpose discussing the salaries of ministers of the Crown, but they are not paid, even in war times, to sit around and let the country run itself. The minister has been a long time in office, and we have never had anything startling from him.
No scandals since I have been here.

No, but if a man is
asleep there can be no scandals-I do not say this offensively. The hon. gentleman is our minister, and we would like to be proud of him in the West. We would like him to have some really startling programme for next session that would show what ia real live minister we have. Whatever might be the case in Ontario, we would like him to show that the Minister of Interior, who 'lives in the prairie provinces, is really on his job. Then, when the question of salaries comes to be considered, as I think it ought to be, we from the West would give the matter favourable consideration.

The hon. gentleman evidently overlooks the fact that this matter had been referred to a commission when he himself suggested that it ought to go to a commission; therefore he ought to qualify his remarks. Whether it is inci-. dental or not, the policy is there all the same. It is something like the policy of protection that my hon. friend used to advocate; it was only incidental, but the protection was there all the same. So, in connection with suggesting a commission, and it has gone to a commission. Of course, I do not think that I ought to anticipate any action of the commission, now that the matter has been referred to them, by making any comments before the commission reports. As' I said before, we cannot expect to do very much in these war times. We have to get through with the war first, at any rate. I admit that we should have a policy promulgated in relation to procedure after the war.
Mr. KNOWLES': I think serious consideration and discussion ought to be given to .these matters in the House long before the war ceases. I think the minister would be justified in appointing a commission, but I do not wish to be understood as saying that that would exhaust his duty.

I have asked the Minister of Financq twice in connection with these railway matters, whether, if this vote of $16,000,000 for the Canadian Northern carries, he intends to ask them to hand over to the Government, in addition to the 40 per cent of the common -stock of the company that the Government now. owns, additional stock to the amount of say $16,000,000 or $20,000,000. I suggest this

not because I consider that this stock would 'be of any particular value, but in order that the Government might be ready to handle the situation and be in
a position to avoid 'being taken by the throat in connection with the matter in the future. My hon. friend is asking for $1)5,000,000 for this company and the company cannot get along without it. The company will hand over that additional stock, which is not now of any commercial value, if my hon. friend the minister insists upon it, and in the interests of the country I think he should insist upon it. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The question that is raised is cognate to the amendment which is being moved by the hon. member for St. John city, and for convenience I had intended to take the two together on Monday.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Upon the assurance given by the hon. member for St. John city that he will facilitate this matter on Monday, we will not waste more time this evening.

Does the hon. gentleman suggest that time was wasted to-night? J do not like that expression "wasting more time." I do not think that the minister would say that time devoted to the consideration of western problems is wasted. The people will be sorry to read that in the Winnipeg 'Telegram on Monday.
